sections.subtitle: Kišno jutro, dobra knjiga i gošća koja je obilježila generacije
sections.screenshot_description: Voditeljica Iva Kraljević predstavlja gošću Željku Horvat Vukelja na početku epizode
sections.content:
Epizodu otvara **Iva Kraljević**, koja gledateljima predstavlja gošću **Željku Horvat Vukelja**. Njezin životni put kreće od **učiteljice francuskog**. Potom je bila dugogodišnja **urednica Modre laste**, a surađivala je i sa SMIB-om. Autorica je stotina dječjih priča i brojnih slikovnica. Kako voditeljica naglašava, generacije su odrasle na pričama i likovima koje je ona osmislila i stavila na papir.

Voditeljica najavljuje teme razgovora:
- zašto su priče djeci toliko važne,
- kako prepoznati dobru, a kako manje kvalitetnu slikovnicu,
- gdje su u svemu tome ekrani i audio bajke,
- kako uskladiti književnu kvalitetu i odgojni, programski sadržaj,
- lektire koje su zastarjele, a ipak nadilaze vrijeme i ostaju na popisima.

Gledatelje poziva da se pretplate na YouTube kanal i podrže njezin rad na platformi Patreon. Napominje da epizodu donosi Cafe Brazil.

Na pitanje kako je, gošća odgovara da je dobro i da je **jutro njezin dio dana**. Navečer joj se srce i mozak još jače rasplamsaju, no tijelo tada više ne sluša kako treba. Iva Kraljević priznaje da nije jutarnji tip. Ipak, kišno jutro tog dana podsjeća je na čitanje: sklupčati se negdje, staviti naočale i uzeti dobru knjigu. Gošća odgovara: „Tako može.“ Tako se razgovor prirodno okreće knjigama, čitanju, a prije svega djeci i pričama.
sections.subtitle_en: A Rainy Morning, a Good Book, and a Guest Who Marked Generations
sections.screenshot_description_en: Host Iva Kraljević introduces guest Željka Horvat Vukelja at the beginning of the episode
sections.content_en:
The episode is opened by **Iva Kraljević**, who introduces the guest **Željka Horvat Vukelja** to the viewers. Her life path starts as a **French teacher**. Afterwards, she was a longtime **editor of Modra lasta**, and she also collaborated with SMIB. She is the author of hundreds of children's stories and numerous picture books. As the host emphasizes, generations grew up on the stories and characters that she conceived and put on paper.

The host announces the topics of conversation:
- why stories are so important to children,
- how to recognize a good picture book, and how a less quality one,
- where screens and audio fairy tales are in all of that,
- how to harmonize literary quality and educational, curriculum content,
- required reading books that are outdated, and yet transcend time and remain on reading lists.

She invites viewers to subscribe to the YouTube channel and support her work on the Patreon platform. She notes that the episode is brought by Cafe Brazil.

To the question of how she is, the guest replies that she is well and that **morning is her part of the day**. In the evening, her heart and brain flare up even stronger, but the body then no longer obeys as it should. Iva Kraljević admits that she is not a morning person. Still, the rainy morning of that day reminds her of reading: curling up somewhere, putting on glasses, and taking a good book. The guest replies: „That works.“ Thus, the conversation naturally turns to books, reading, and above all to children and stories.

sections.subtitle: Tatino večernje čitanje i lutka koja je ostala na grani
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Horvat Vukelja prisjeća se priče s tužnim krajem koju joj je otac čitao
sections.content:
Na pitanje koje su je priče odgojile, Željka Horvat Vukelja odgovara: **klasične priče**, najmanje jedna svaki dan. Čitao joj ih je otac. Opisuje to kao „klasični brak“: majka je radila sve u kući, a kasnije, kad se zaposlila, i izvan nje. Otac je čitao, šetao, razmišljao i puno se bavio njezinim odrastanjem.

Otac nije bio pripovjedač i čitao je bez velike glume, ali, kako kaže, očito s ljubavlju. Djevojčica je znala da će sve biti onako kako je tata obećao. Čitali su velike slikovnice s poznatim pričama koje je ilustrirao **Vladimir Kirin**.

Gošću zanimljivim čini to što je **nije užasavalo** da vuk pojede Crvenkapicu ni koliko su zle maćehe u Pepeljugi i Snjeguljici. Te su se priče čitale polako i mirno. Nije imala velikih pitanja, samo je čekala večernju priču.

Jedna priča ipak je bila drukčija. U transkriptu se njezin naslov bilježi kao „Halugica Jablanko“, a nije čak bila ni bogato ilustrirana. Završavala je nesretno: djevojčici je lutka ostala negdje na stablu. Gošća je bila jako nesretna jer je to, kako naglašava, bila **priča iz stvarnog života**. Kao da je naslutila preneseno značenje. Daleke i napete bajke nisu je brinule, a ova jest.

Otac je zato smislio novi kraj, sastavljen „iz raznih priča“ najbolje što je mogao. **Mljekarica**, koje su tada kući donosile mlijeko, pronašla je lutkicu i vratila je djevojčici. Gošća tu priču više nikad nije tražila, iz straha da lutka opet ne ostane na grani.

Iva Kraljević primjećuje kako djeca prepoznaju kad je priča realna i kad ih to potrese. Najavljuje da će se kasnije vratiti na pitanje trebaju li roditelji i pripovjedači u takvim trenucima intervenirati.
sections.subtitle_en: Dad's Evening Reading and the Doll That Remained on the Branch
sections.screenshot_description_en: Željka Horvat Vukelja recalls a story with a sad ending that her father used to read to her
sections.content_en:
To the question of which stories raised her, Željka Horvat Vukelja answers: **classic stories**, at least one every day. Her father read them to her. She describes it as a „classic marriage“: her mother did everything in the house, and later, when she got a job, outside of it as well. Her father read, walked, reflected, and engaged greatly with her growing up.

Her father was not a storyteller and read without great theatricality, but, as she says, clearly with love. The little girl knew that everything would be as dad promised. They read large picture books with well-known stories illustrated by **Vladimir Kirin**.

What the guest finds interesting is that **it did not terrify her** that the wolf eats Little Red Riding Hood, nor how evil stepmothers are in Cinderella and Snow White. Those stories were read slowly and calmly. She did not have big questions, she just waited for the evening story.

One story, however, was different. In the transcript, its title is recorded as „Halugica Jablanko“, and it was not even richly illustrated. It ended sadly: the little girl's doll remained somewhere on a tree. The guest was very unhappy because that, as she emphasizes, was a **story from real life**. It was as if she sensed the metaphorical meaning. Distant and suspenseful fairy tales did not worry her, but this one did.

Her father therefore devised a new ending, composed „from various stories“ as best he could. The **milkmaid**, who back then brought milk to homes, found the little doll and returned it to the girl. The guest never asked for that story again, out of fear that the doll would remain on the branch again.

Iva Kraljević observes how children recognize when a story is realistic and when it shakes them. She announces that they will return later to the question of whether parents and storytellers should intervene in such moments.

sections.subtitle: Od Vjesnikove nagradice do uredničke fotelje Modre laste
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća se prisjeća prvih objavljenih radova i sna o novinarstvu
sections.content:
Iva Kraljević podsjeća da je gošća priče pisala još kao gimnazijalka i da joj je jedna tada objavljena u **Modroj lasti**. Kasnije je ondje bila urednica gotovo trideset godina, prema podacima koje je voditeljica pronašla od 1982. do 2014. Gošća potvrđuje uz osmijeh: „Bolje od mene sve znate.“

Priznaje da je o tome sanjala, još davno u **Zadru**, gdje je bila članica literarne grupe. Novinarskih grupa tada nije bilo. Željela je objavljivati u novinama, pa su joj mali članci izlazili u **Zadarskom narodnom listu**. **Vjesnik** je imao stranicu za dječje radove i suradnje. Jednom je ondje dobila nagradu za mali filmski sinopsis: fotoalbum sa zlatnom etiketom i natpisom nagrade Vjesnika. „Pa to je meni cijeli svijet predstavljalo“, prisjeća se.

Mislila je da će biti novinarka. Danas kaže da „srećom“ nije, jer je to danas težak i nezahvalan kruh. Ipak je na neki način završila u novinarstvu. Modra lasta nije klasična novina, nego **edukativni, pa i umjetnički časopis**. U njemu se moglo svašta kombinirati, urednik je imao slobodne ruke, a kolektiv je uvijek nalazio dobra rješenja.

Prije toga je **devet godina radila kao učiteljica** u osnovnoj školi, s djecom od prvog do osmog razreda. To naziva vrlo dragocjenim iskustvom.
sections.subtitle_en: From Vjesnik's Little Prize to the Editorial Chair of Modra lasta
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest recalls her first published works and the dream of journalism
sections.content_en:
Iva Kraljević recalls that the guest wrote stories back when she was a high school student and that one was published back then in **Modra lasta**. Later she was an editor there for nearly thirty years, according to information found by the host from 1982 to 2014. The guest confirms with a smile: „You know everything better than I do.“

She admits that she dreamed of it, long ago in **Zadar**, where she was a member of a literary group. Journalism groups did not exist back then. She wanted to publish in newspapers, so her little articles were published in **Zadarski narodni list**. **Vjesnik** had a page for children's works and contributions. Once she received an award there for a little film synopsis: a photo album with a golden label and an inscription of the Vjesnik prize. „Why, that represented the whole world to me,“ she recalls.

She thought she would be a journalist. Today she says that „fortunately“ she is not, because today that is a hard and thankless bread. Still, in a way she ended up in journalism. Modra lasta is not a classic newspaper, but an **educational, even artistic magazine**. All sorts of things could be combined in it, the editor had a free hand, and the collective always found good solutions.

Before that, she **worked as a teacher for nine years** in elementary school, with children from first to eighth grade. She calls that a very precious experience.

sections.subtitle: Modra lasta među djecom: više od 2000 susreta
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Horvat Vukelja govori o više od 2000 susreta s djecom
sections.content:
U Modroj lasti zatekla je, kako kaže, divnu redakciju i prekrasne ljude od kojih je mnogo naučila. Prihvatila je sve što se ondje i prije radilo. Unijela je jednu novost: **da Modra lasta ide među djecu**. Kolege su to činile povremeno i rjeđe, a ona je jedina među njima bila učiteljica iz prakse.

Išla je u škole s edukativnim predavanjima uz postere časopisa. Jedan je bio poster za djevojčice s nekoliko važnih savjeta o izgledu, zbog kojih bi je danas, kaže, valjda ismijali. Drugi je donosio **deset pravila o tome kako učiti**. Gošća primjećuje da su danas o tome napisane cijele knjige, a tada toga nije bilo. Bili su inovatori malim prilozima koji su djeci davali materijal za razmišljanje.

Kad joj je **Školska knjiga** počela izdavati slikovnice, počela je djeci pričati priče. To smatra svojim pravim područjem, onim na kojem je najplodnija i ima najveće zasluge. Tako, ističe, zaista dopire do djece.

Brojke govore same za sebe. Iza nje je **više od 2000 susreta**. Svaki traje jedan školski sat, a na svakom je pedesetak djece, ponekad i puno više. Poziva slušatelje da zamisle koliko je to djece i učiteljica.
sections.subtitle_en: Modra lasta Among Children: More Than 2,000 Encounters
sections.screenshot_description_en: Željka Horvat Vukelja speaks about more than 2,000 encounters with children
sections.content_en:
In Modra lasta she found, as she says, a wonderful editorial team and beautiful people from whom she learned a lot. She accepted everything that had been done there before. She introduced one novelty: **for Modra lasta to go among children**. Her colleagues did that occasionally and more rarely, and she was the only one among them who was a teacher from practice.

She went to schools with educational lectures accompanied by magazine posters. One was a poster for girls with several important pieces of advice about appearance, for which today, she says, she would probably be mocked. The other brought **ten rules on how to study**. The guest remarks that today entire books have been written about that, and back then there was none of that. They were innovators with small contributions that gave children food for thought.

When **Školska knjiga** began publishing her picture books, she began telling stories to children. She considers that her true area, the one in which she is most fruitful and has the greatest merits. That way, she points out, she truly reaches children.

The numbers speak for themselves. Behind her are **more than 2,000 encounters**. Each lasts one school class period, and at each there are about fifty children, sometimes even many more. She invites listeners to imagine how many children and teachers that is.

sections.subtitle: Dječak u krem trenirci: kako se bori za izgubljenu pažnju
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća prepričava anegdotu o nemirnom dječaku iz OŠ Žitnjak
sections.content:
Iva Kraljević pita što radi kad u publici vidi dijete koje je izgubila. Bori li se za njega ili ga pušta? „Borim se“, odgovara gošća, **ali ne opominje**. Od opominjanja je odustala već nakon drugog ili trećeg puta. Najprije se pravi da ne vidi. Zatim nešto okrene, skrati neki dio ili unese nešto novo.

Za to ima upečatljiv primjer iz **Osnovne škole Žitnjak**, gdje joj je publika inače uvijek bila odlična. Jedan dječak došao je uredan i mirisan, u lijepoj bijeloj ili krem trenirci sa zelenim mrljama na koljenima, jer se već negdje hrvao u travi. Kad je počela pričati o dječaku koji nije volio prati uši pa su mu iz njih izrasle biljke, okrenuo se drugima: „**To vam je laž. Sve laže. Sve je izmislila.**“ Ostalu djecu to je smetalo.

Gošća iskreno priznaje da bi ga najradije uhvatila za trenirku i protresla, „ali ne smiješ“. Rekla je sebi: „Željka, ti moraš biti još dvostruko zanimljivija.“ Ubacila je malo dramskoga i dječak ju je do kraja slušao otvorenih usta. Kaže da joj je zapravo pomogao **doraditi priče i nastup**.

Mogla ga je opomenuti ili prijaviti učiteljici. Cijeni učiteljice koje nemirno dijete samo strateški premjeste. Inače sve rješava neizravno, što traži dodatni trud. Povlači paralelu s roditeljstvom, u kojem neke stvari također traže dodatni angažman roditelja. Zaključuje: **uvijek se isplati**.
sections.subtitle_en: The Boy in the Cream Tracksuit: How One Fights for Lost Attention
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest recounts an anecdote about a restless boy from Primary School Žitnjak
sections.content_en:
Iva Kraljević asks what she does when in the audience she sees a child she has lost. Does she fight for him or let him go? „I fight,“ replies the guest, **but does not admonish**. She gave up admonishing already after the second or third time. First she pretends not to see. Then she turns something around, shortens some part, or introduces something new.

For this she has a striking example from **Osnovna škola Žitnjak**, where her audience was otherwise always excellent. One boy came tidy and fragrant, in a nice white or cream tracksuit with green stains on the knees, because he had already wrestled somewhere in the grass. When she began telling about a boy who did not like to wash his ears so plants grew out of them, he turned to the others: „**That's a lie to you. She lies about everything. She made it all up.**“ That bothered the other children.

The guest honestly admits that she would have liked best to grab him by the tracksuit and shake him, „but you must not.“ She told herself: „Željka, you must be twice as interesting.“ She inserted a bit of theatrical drama and the boy listened to her until the end with an open mouth. She says that he actually helped her **refine the stories and performance**.

She could have admonished him or reported him to the teacher. She appreciates teachers who merely strategically move a restless child. Otherwise she resolves everything indirectly, which requires additional effort. She draws a parallel with parenting, in which some things also require additional engagement from parents. She concludes: **it is always worth it**.

sections.subtitle: Djeca su ista u srži, mijenja se svijet oko njih
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Horvat Vukelja objašnjava kako kontekst oko djece utječe na njihovu pažnju
sections.content:
Voditeljica pita mijenjaju li se djeca s vremenom ili su u svojoj srži ista. Gošći se sviđa riječ „srž“. Odgovara da se pripovjedač mora mijenjati jer se i djeca mijenjaju, ali **njihova se bit nije promijenila**. Djeca od pet do osam godina i dalje su razigrana, živahna, radoznala, otvorena, autentična i iskrena. Ne brinu o tome kakav će dojam ostaviti.

Ponekad je neko dijete želi impresionirati znanjem. U **Kutini** je tako saznala kolikom brzinom puž puže u pet ili deset minuta. To je, kaže, bilo fantastično, a dijete s pravom ponosno. No većinom djeca ne žele impresionirati, nego **proučavati odrasle**. Zato sve kažu otvoreno, pa i pitanje „Kak ste vi stari?“. Učiteljicama je to neugodno, a gošća to smatra normalnim.

Promijenio se **kontekst oko djece**, i on ih, kako kaže, malo nagriza. Djeca su danas kraće pažnje, pa priča više ne može teći sporo. U manjoj, komornijoj skupini još su spremna za klasično slušanje. Veća skupina dođe nakon tjelesnog ili nakon čekanja onih s vjeronauka, pa je previše razigrana. Tek što se smire, zazvoni.

Zato prilagođava priče i nastup, iako naglašava da **nije glumica** ni prava lutkarica, nego „priučena“. Ima rekvizite i kartonske lutke, ali nikakve specijalne efekte. Jednom su je najavili kao predstavu. Dok je već pričala, djevojčica iz prvog reda upitala je: „**A kad će predstava?**“ A predstava je već bila to.

Njezin je recept da bude **mozaična**: kratki dijelovi koji se izmjenjuju. Želi da i učiteljice pritom predahnu i ponesu neku ideju, kao što ona od njih uzima ideje s panoa ili način na koji smiruju razred. To naziva **tihom razmjenom**. Djeca su ipak uvijek u prvom planu.
sections.subtitle_en: Children Are the Same at the Core, the World Around Them Changes
sections.screenshot_description_en: Željka Horvat Vukelja explains how the context around children affects their attention
sections.content_en:
The host asks whether children change with time or are the same at their core. The guest likes the word „core“. She replies that the storyteller must change because children change as well, but **their essence has not changed**. Children aged five to eight are still playful, lively, curious, open, authentic, and sincere. They do not worry about what impression they will make.

Sometimes a child wants to impress her with knowledge. In **Kutina** she thus found out at what speed a snail crawls in five or ten minutes. That, she says, was fantastic, and the child rightfully proud. But mostly children do not want to impress, but rather **to study adults**. That is why they say everything openly, including the question „How come you're old?“. Teachers find that awkward, and the guest considers it normal.

The **context around children** has changed, and it, as she says, erodes them a bit. Children today have a shorter attention span, so the story can no longer flow slowly. In a smaller, more chamber group they are still ready for classic listening. A larger group comes after physical education or after waiting for those from religious instruction, so it is overly playful. Barely have they calmed down, the bell rings.

That is why she adapts stories and the performance, although she emphasizes that **she is not an actress** nor a real puppeteer, but „self-trained“. She has props and cardboard puppets, but no special effects. Once she was announced as a play. While she was already telling, a girl from the first row asked: „**And when is the play going to be?**“ And the play was already that.

Her recipe is to be **mosaic-like**: short parts that alternate. She wants teachers to catch their breath at the same time and take away some idea, just as she takes ideas from them from notice boards or the way they calm the class. She calls that a **quiet exchange**. Children are nevertheless always in the foreground.

sections.subtitle: Zaboravit ćemo imena i brojke, ali ne i doživljaj
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća objašnjava zašto je priča prije svega doživljaj
sections.content:
Na pitanje zašto je priča uopće važna i što daje djetetu, gošća odgovara sažeto: **zato što je priča doživljaj**. Odmah dodaje da to nije njezina misao. Time su se bavili psiholozi, a mnogi su je kasnije ponavljali.

Objašnjava kako pamćenje funkcionira. Zaboravit ćemo nečiji lik, ime, godinu i brojke, čak i mjesto gdje se nešto događalo. Ali to da nam je negdje bilo lijepo ili ružno **zadnje ćemo zaboraviti**. To ostaje u nama, svjesno ili nesvjesno. Zato je važno da nešto lijepo doživimo, a priča bi to morala biti.

Razlikuje doživljaj od pukog veselja. Djeca prepoznaju kad se odrasli malo „ogluparaju“: netko padne na bananu, iznenadi ih neki zvuk, nešto ih nasmije. Gošća se tada i sama smije poput djeteta. Veselje je dragocjeno, ali **ne može dugo trajati**. Lijepo je, zaključuje, kad iza njega ostane pravi doživljaj.
sections.subtitle_en: We Will Forget Names and Numbers, but Not the Experience
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest explains why a story is above all an experience
sections.content_en:
To the question of why a story is important at all and what it gives to a child, the guest replies concisely: **because a story is an experience**. She immediately adds that this is not her thought. Psychologists have dealt with that, and many later repeated it.

She explains how memory functions. We will forget someone's appearance, name, year, and numbers, even the place where something happened. But that it was nice or ugly for us somewhere **we will forget last**. That remains in us, consciously or unconsciously. That is why it is important that we experience something nice, and a story ought to be that.

She distinguishes an experience from mere merriment. Children recognize when adults „act a bit silly“: someone slips on a banana, some sound surprises them, something makes them laugh. The guest then laughs herself like a child. Merriment is precious, but **it cannot last long**. It is nice, she concludes, when a true experience remains behind it.

sections.subtitle: Problemske slikovnice i četiri miša iz HNK-a
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Horvat Vukelja opisuje svoju neobjavljenu slikovnicu o miševima u kazalištu
sections.content:
Iva Kraljević pita može li priča biti pozitivan doživljaj ako je istodobno opomena. Danas izlazi mnogo izrazito odgojnih slikovnica, pa se pita jesu li namijenjene djetetu ili roditelju koji treba pomoć da nešto iskomunicira. Gošća hvali pitanja i objašnjava da se takve slikovnice nekad učeno zvale **problemske**. Kad je prvi put shvatila da je i sama napisala jednu takvu, kaže, nije ni znala da je to učinila.

Takvih slikovnica treba biti, smatra ona, ali izdavači danas **traže uglavnom njih jer se kupuju**. Voditeljica dodaje da roditelji biraju takve naslove jer im treba pomoć.

Gošća otkriva da ima **najmanje deset spremnih tekstova**, u glavi već napola prelomljenih za slikovnicu, s mislima o tome kakve mogućnosti nude ilustratoru. Svi su veseli. Cilj im je upoznati djecu s nečim lijepim, a korist dolazi usput.

Jedan od njih govori o **četiri miša koja žive u kazalištu HNK**, sve dok jednog dana ne stigne mačka primadone. Nastaje revolucija u kazalištu, što podsjeća na Toma i Jerryja, iako nije posve to. Priča bez ijedne eksplicitne poruke pokazuje kako su se likovi ipak mogli dogovoriti i kako ih glazba okuplja. Djeci prenosi ljepotu glazbe i želju da zavire u HNK ili bilo koje pravo kazalište.

Za takve tekstove, kaže, nema mnogo šanse kod izdavača. To vrijedi iako je poznato ime u tom području i iako izdavači znaju da će slikovnicu sama predstavljati. Teško se probije tekst kojem je cilj samo da se djeca vesele: uvijek „mora biti još nešto“.
sections.subtitle_en: Problem Picture Books and the Four Mice from the HNK
sections.screenshot_description_en: Željka Horvat Vukelja describes her unpublished picture book about mice in the theater
sections.content_en:
Iva Kraljević asks whether a story can be a positive experience if it is simultaneously an admonition. Today many distinctly educational picture books come out, so she wonders whether they are intended for the child or for the parent who needs help to communicate something. The guest praises the questions and explains that such picture books were once scholarly called **problem-based**. When she first realized that she herself had written one such, she says, she didn't even know she had done it.

There should be such picture books, she believes, but publishers today **seek mostly them because they sell**. The host adds that parents choose such titles because they need help.

The guest reveals that she has **at least ten texts ready**, in her head already half laid out for a picture book, with thoughts about what possibilities they offer to an illustrator. All are cheerful. Their goal is to introduce children to something nice, and the benefit comes along the way.

One of them speaks about **four mice that live in the HNK theater**, until one day the prima donna's cat arrives. A revolution ensues in the theater, which is reminiscent of Tom and Jerry, although it is not entirely that. The story, without a single explicit message, shows how the characters were nevertheless able to reach an agreement and how music brings them together. It conveys to children the beauty of music and the desire to peek into the HNK or any real theater.

For such texts, she says, there is not much chance with publishers. This holds true even though she is a well-known name in that field and even though publishers know that she will present the picture book herself. It is hard for a text whose only goal is for children to rejoice to break through: there always „must be something more“.

> "Magisterium alignment:" N/A

sections.subtitle: Stručni i dječji žiri: kad profinjenost ne dopre do djeteta
sections.screenshot_description: Razgovor o razlici između izbora stručnog i dječjeg žirija
sections.content:
Gošća prati nagrade sajma u **Bologni** i **nagradu Astrid Lindgren**. Spominje da je i sama dvije godine bila uključena zajedno sa **Sanjom Pirić**, a da je ranije u ime Hrvatske kandidatkinja bila **Jelena Pervan**. Nagrađuju se slikovnice koje su krasna umjetnička djela, s mnogo minimalizma, dizajnerske profinjenosti i suptilnih **sivih tonova**. Kod djece to, upozorava, ne prolazi baš, osim ako ih se posebno educira i senzibilizira. Malo koji roditelj to može, jer ni sam ne zna. Zato poziva da se gleda prosječno dijete.

Iva Kraljević primjećuje da su u Hrvatskoj i 2024. i 2025. **stručni žiri i dječji žiri izabrali različite naslove**. Gošća kaže da bi bila sretna kad bi joj nagradu dao upravo dječji žiri. Poštuje i stručne žirije. I sama je nekoliko puta bila u njima i drago joj je da nije češće, jer je dodjeljivanje nagrada kolegama vrlo delikatno i odgovorno. Ipak, priznaje da svaka nagrada piscu dobro dođe. Uspoređuje to s mladim pijanistima, koji bez određenog broja hrvatskih i svjetskih nagrada ne mogu dalje.

Voditeljica dijeli osobno iskustvo. Sinu je čitala estetski lijepu, minimalističku slikovnicu, misleći da je to dobro jer djeci pažnja ne treba ići na sto strana. Sin ju je upitao **zašto je sve okolo prazno**. Gošća to smatra posve normalnim pitanjem.
sections.subtitle_en: Expert and Children's Jury: When Refinement Fails to Reach the Child
sections.screenshot_description_en: Conversation about the difference between the choice of the expert and children's jury
sections.content_en:
The guest follows the awards of the fair in **Bologna** and the **Astrid Lindgren Award**. She mentions that she herself was involved for two years together with **Sanja Pirić**, and that earlier on behalf of Croatia the nominee was **Jelena Pervan**. Picture books that are wonderful works of art are awarded, with a lot of minimalism, designer refinement, and subtle **gray tones**. With children that, she warns, doesn't really go down well, unless they are specially educated and sensitized. Very few parents can do that, because they themselves do not know. Therefore she calls for looking at the average child.

Iva Kraljević observes that in Croatia in both 2024 and 2025 **the expert jury and the children's jury chose different titles**. The guest says that she would be happy if the children's jury were precisely the one to give her an award. She also respects expert juries. She herself was on them several times and is glad that she was not more often, because awarding prizes to colleagues is very delicate and responsible. Nevertheless, she admits that every award comes in handy for a writer. She compares that to young pianists, who cannot move forward without a certain number of Croatian and world awards.

The host shares a personal experience. She read an aesthetically beautiful, minimalist picture book to her son, thinking that was good because children's attention should not go in a hundred directions. Her son asked her **why everything around is empty**. The guest considers that a completely normal question.

sections.subtitle: Pauk koji se otkriva tek pri drugom čitanju
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća opisuje radost djece kad u bogatoj ilustraciji otkriju sporednu priču
sections.content:
Gošća zagovara da postoje **i minimalističke, profinjene slikovnice**, ali i one koje kritičari s malo nipodaštavanja nazivaju „komercijalnima“. U tu skupinu, kaže, smještaju i nju kad napiše nešto što se dobro prodaje. Postoji i treća razina: slikovnice toliko „nabrijane“ bojama i **snishodljive prema djeci** da to svi prepoznaju, osim roditelja koji nije u tom svijetu. Ne zamjera to roditeljima, jer svatko ima svoje područje. Takve su slikovnice privlačne „na prvu loptu“, pa i preprivlačne.

Najviše cijeni **srednje područje**: vedre i vesele slikovnice. Djeca vole čak i pretrpane ilustracije u kojima pri drugom čitanju otkriju pauka koji gore nešto plete. Na sljedećoj stranici taj pauk nešto spušta na glavu sporednog lika. Usporedo se odvija još jedna priča, a djeca su, kaže, **presretna kad je pronađu**.

Mnoge slikovnice u sivim tonovima i suženom rasponu boja zapravo su slikovnice za odrasle. Francuzi i Belgijanci, a možda i drugi, to imaju kao posebnu kategoriju. Gošća nije protiv toga, ali poručuje: „**Nemojmo samo takve nagrađivati.** Zanemarimo ono što djeca vole.“

Dodaje i napomenu o dječjim žirijima: na djecu od osam ili devet godina lako je utjecati jer upijaju ono što im odrasli kažu. S trinaest ili četrnaest godina sve rade obratno. To nije tragično, jer će se, kaže, vratiti. Zaključuje da je za to da postoje različiti pristupi. Ima svoj, ali o drugima duboko razmišlja.
sections.subtitle_en: A Spider Discovered Only on Second Reading
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest describes the joy of children when they discover a secondary storyline in a rich illustration
sections.content_en:
The guest advocates that there should be **both minimalist, refined picture books**, but also those that critics call „commercial“ with a bit of disdain. Into that group, she says, they place her as well when she writes something that sells well. There is also a third level: picture books so „hyped up“ with colors and **condescending toward children** that everyone recognizes it, except the parent who is not in that world. She does not hold that against parents, because everyone has their own field. Such picture books are attractive „at first glance“, even overly attractive.

She appreciates most the **middle ground**: bright and cheerful picture books. Children even love overcrowded illustrations in which on the second reading they discover a spider weaving something up above. On the next page that spider lowers something onto the head of a secondary character. A parallel story unfolds, and children are, she says, **overjoyed when they find it**.

Many picture books in gray tones and a narrowed range of colors are actually picture books for adults. The French and Belgians, and perhaps others, have that as a separate category. The guest is not against that, but conveys: „**Let us not award only those.** Let us not neglect what children love.“

She also adds a note about children's juries: children of eight or nine years are easy to influence because they absorb what adults tell them. At thirteen or fourteen years they do everything the opposite way. That is not tragic, because, she says, they will return. She concludes that she is in favor of having different approaches. She has hers, but thinks deeply about others.

sections.subtitle: Je li vuk stvarno progutao baku? Ne trebamo biti preanalitični
sections.screenshot_description: Iva Kraljević pita jesu li stare bajke prestrašne za današnju djecu
sections.content:
Iva Kraljević priznaje da joj se starije bajke ponekad čine strašnijima od onoga što se danas nudi djeci. Već kod **Tri praščića** ne zna kako završiti, a kod **Crvenkapice** se pita je li vuk doista progutao cijelu baku ili se baka sakrila. U **Sedam kozlića** vuk na kraju upadne u bunar, a djeca pitaju što je s njim bilo. Pita jesu li te priče prestrašne ili smo mi danas preosjetljivi.

Gošća odgovara: „**Ili smo preanalitični.**“ Previše razmišljamo o tome kako ćemo nešto predstaviti. Ako se priča klasično, onako kako je njoj otac čitao, nema detalja. Vuk je progutao baku i plovi se dalje, ali nitko neće opisivati kako je žvakao.

Priznaje da današnju djecu **učimo postavljati pitanja** i da je na tome izgrađen cijeli školski kurikulum. To je dobro, no kad dijete krene u analizu, pripovjedač je u nevolji. Tada se snalazi kako zna, a roditelj svoje dijete poznaje najbolje.

Iz odgoja vlastite djece nudi praktičan savjet: ako niste spremni za objašnjenje, **svratite pažnju** na nešto drugo. Opisuje dijete koje se u dućanu baci na pod jer mu se nešto ne kupi. Roditelj ga može pustiti i reći „Ja idem, ti ostani“, pa dijete gotovo uvijek dođe za njim. Ako mu je to prestrogo, može se „sjetiti“ da susjeda ima rođendan i da joj treba kupiti dar. Za to treba glumiti i domisliti se makar banalne stvari, ali pažnja će otići dalje, osim u ekstremnim slučajevima. Njezina je poruka jednostavna: **ne komplicirati, nego pričati**.
sections.subtitle_en: Did the Wolf Really Swallow Grandma? We Need Not Be Overly Analytical
sections.screenshot_description_en: Iva Kraljević asks whether old fairy tales are too scary for today's children
sections.content_en:
Iva Kraljević admits that older fairy tales sometimes seem scarier to her than what is offered to children today. Already with the **Three Little Pigs** she does not know how to finish, and with **Little Red Riding Hood** she wonders whether the wolf truly swallowed the whole grandmother or grandmother hid. In the **Seven Little Goats** the wolf falls into the well at the end, and the children ask what happened to him. She asks whether those stories are too scary or we today are oversensitive.

The guest replies: „**Or we are overly analytical.**“ We think too much about how we will present something. If a story is told classically, the way her father read to her, there are no details. The wolf swallowed grandmother and one sails on, but no one will describe how he chewed.

She admits that today's children **we teach to ask questions** and that the entire school curriculum is built on that. That is good, but when a child sets out into analysis, the storyteller is in trouble. Then one manages as one knows how, and a parent knows their child best.

From raising her own children she offers practical advice: if you are not ready for an explanation, **divert attention** to something else. She describes a child who throws himself on the floor in a store because something is not bought for him. A parent can let him be and say „I am going, you stay“, and the child almost always follows. If that is too strict for him, one can „remember“ that the neighbor has a birthday and needs a gift bought. For that one needs to act and come up with even a banal thing, but the attention will move on, except in extreme cases. Her message is simple: **do not complicate, but tell stories**.

sections.subtitle: Labuđe jezero: kad glazba iscijeli tugu, a djeca biraju kraj
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća pripovijeda kako je predškolcima ispričala Labuđe jezero uz glazbu i fotografije
sections.content:
Kao lijep primjer kako se nositi s tužnim završetkom, gošća navodi **Labuđe jezero**, koje završava nesretno: labud umire jer je bio drukčiji. Priču je ispričala u glazbaonici, privatnoj glazbenoj školi u kojoj je radila, **predškolcima** i nekolicini učenika prvog razreda.

Pripremila se temeljito. Pomogla se **monografijom Hrvatskog narodnog kazališta** s velikim, umjetničkim fotografijama labudica. S jedne strane pokazivala je crtane junake na kartonu, a s druge fotografije balerina, pa je sve to isprepletala. Djeca su prije toga slušala lijepu glazbu i gledala, među ostalim, ples četiri balerinice.

Ispričala im je da labud umire i da je to zadnja scena. Djeca su bila tužna, ali gošća kaže da ih je **koda iscijelila**. Sve je bilo nježno i uz mnogo glazbe u pozadini.

Potom je dobila prevedenu slikovnicu **Školske knjige** s gumbima koji puštaju arije, u kojoj je završetak sretan i nježan. Djeci je rekla da kraj može biti i takav. Prihvatili su obje verzije i rekli da im se svima više sviđa sretni kraj. Gošća im je odgovorila: „Pa mi ćemo to. **To je i onako sve izmišljeno.**“ Naglašava da je ključ bila brižljiva priprema: djeca nisu u priču uvedena iznenada.
sections.subtitle_en: Swan Lake: When Music Heals Sadness, and Children Choose the Ending
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest recounts how she told Swan Lake to preschoolers with music and photographs
sections.content_en:
As a nice example of how to handle a sad ending, the guest cites **Swan Lake**, which ends unhappily: the swan dies because it was different. She told the story in a music playroom, a private music school where she worked, to **preschoolers** and a few first-grade pupils.

She prepared thoroughly. She made use of a **monograph of the Croatian National Theatre** with large, artistic photographs of swans. On one side she showed cartoon characters on cardboard, and on the other photographs of ballerinas, and so she intertwined all that. Before that, the children listened to beautiful music and watched, among other things, the dance of the four little ballerinas.

She told them that the swan dies and that this is the final scene. The children were sad, but the guest says that the **coda healed them**. Everything was gentle and with plenty of music in the background.

Afterwards she received a translated picture book from **Školska knjiga** with buttons that play arias, in which the ending is happy and gentle. She told the children that the ending could be like that too. They accepted both versions and said that they all preferred the happy ending. The guest replied to them: „Well, we will do that. **It is all made up anyway.**“ She emphasizes that the key was careful preparation: the children were not introduced into the story suddenly.

sections.subtitle: Mogu li stabla govoriti? Umjetnici kao prevoditelji jezika stvari
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Horvat Vukelja objašnjava dječaku da pisci prevode jezik biljaka
sections.content:
I izmišljenost priče može biti izazov, kako je gošća doživjela u osnovnoj školi u **Dugavama**. Ispričala je smiješnu priču o ljubavi između dva stabla koja govore i razmišljaju. Djeca su pljeskala, a onda se javio dječak iz prvog razreda. Najprije ju je pristojno pohvalio, a zatim rekao: „Ja se isto pitam. **Pa ne mogu stabla govoriti.**“ Gošća kaže da joj to nitko nikad nije rekao tako suvislo i lijepo.

Odgovorila mu je da **biljke međusobno komuniciraju** i navela dva ili tri primjera, među ostalim komunikaciju korijenjem. Objasnila je da biljke govore svojim jezikom koji ljudi ne razumiju. Razumiju ga pisci i drugi umjetnici: ilustratori i oni koji rade crtiće. Ona se kao spisateljica uživi u njih i prevede djeci. Zaključila je: „Zato služe umjetnici, **da nam prevode jezik stvari**, jezik biljaka i životinja“, i to na hrvatski jezik.

Učiteljice su odahnule jer su mislile da je u nevolji. Čak je i predstavnica izdavača, koja ju je slušala već stotinu puta i obično radi nešto u pozadini, zastala da vidi kako će to riješiti.

Gošća ipak povlači granicu. Djeci neće prerano otkriti tajnu **svetog Nikole**, Djeda Božićnjaka ni Djeda Mraza, kako god ga zvali. To trebaju shvatiti postupno. Drago joj je što je jezik biljaka uspjela objasniti na ovaj način.
sections.subtitle_en: Can Trees Talk? Artists as Translators of the Language of Things
sections.screenshot_description_en: Željka Horvat Vukelja explains to a boy that writers translate the language of plants
sections.content_en:
The fictionality of a story can also be a challenge, as the guest experienced in an elementary school in **Dugave**. She told a funny story about love between two trees that talk and think. The children applauded, and then a first-grade boy spoke up. First he complimented her politely, and then said: „I wonder too. **Why, trees cannot talk.**“ The guest says that no one had ever said that to her so coherently and nicely.

She answered him that **plants communicate with each other** and cited two or three examples, among others communication through roots. She explained that plants speak their own language that humans do not understand. Writers and other artists understand it: illustrators and those who make cartoons. As a writer, she puts herself in their shoes and translates for children. She concluded: „That is what artists are for, **to translate for us the language of things**, the language of plants and animals“, and that into the Croatian language.

The teachers sighed in relief because they thought she was in trouble. Even the publisher's representative, who had listened to her a hundred times already and usually does something in the background, paused to see how she would solve that.

The guest nevertheless draws a line. She will not reveal the secret of **Saint Nicholas**, Santa Claus, or Father Frost, whatever one calls him, to children too early. They need to grasp that gradually. She is glad that she managed to explain the language of plants in this way.

sections.subtitle: Mora li svaka priča imati pouku? Dječak koji nije prao uši
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća pripovijeda nastanak priče o dječaku kojem su iz ušiju izrasle grane
sections.content:
Iva Kraljević pita opterećuje li je unaprijed pouka i treba li je uopće svaka priča imati. Gošća odgovara da **ne mora nužno**, ali da je to opterećuje. Zato tekstove daje kolegicama i urednicima i uvažava primjedbe kad smatra da su opravdane.

Kao primjer navodi priču o dječaku kojemu su **iz ušiju izrasle grane jer ih nije prao**. Izmislila ju je za svog učenika francuskog, kojeg opisuje kao najboljeg učenika i krasnog dječaka. Uvijek je imao „marmeladu od marelice“ u ušima, vjerojatno zato što nije dao da mu se peru. Danas je, kaže, poznati liječnik i možda više ni ne zna da je priča bila o njemu.

Prvo pričanje dobro je prošlo. Dječak je slušao otvorenih usta, a vrećicu s papučicama objesio je toliko neobično da ga je morala upozoriti: „To nije kuka.“ Sutradan, pregledavajući zadaću, primijetila je da su mu **uši čiste**.

Kad je priča izašla kao slikovnica i kad ju je predstavljala djeci, dogodilo se nešto neočekivano. U jednom malom mjestu u **Prigorju** jednom je dječaku toliko pozlilo da su ga morali iznijeti ispred škole na zidić. Očito ni on nije volio prati uši. Gošća zaključuje da je bila **predrastična**. Otada priči uvijek prethodi uvod u kojem objašnjava da ju je izmislila za svog učenika.

Iz toga je naučila da uvijek nastupa nježno. Ako u publici ima djece s autizmom, ne govori preglasno, iako je inače glasan tip. „Sve zaobljeno mora biti“, kaže. Ističe da stalno uči i nastoji se poboljšavati.
sections.subtitle_en: Must Every Story Have a Moral? The Boy Who Did Not Wash His Ears
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest recounts the origin of the story about the boy from whose ears branches grew
sections.content_en:
Iva Kraljević asks whether a moral burdens her in advance and whether every story needs to have one at all. The guest replies that **it does not necessarily have to**, but that it burdens her. That is why she gives texts to colleagues and editors and respects objections when she considers them justified.

As an example, she cites the story about the boy from whose **ears branches grew because he did not wash them**. She made it up for her French student, whom she describes as the best student and a wonderful boy. He always had „apricot jam“ in his ears, probably because he did not let them be washed. Today, she says, he is a well-known physician and perhaps no longer even knows that the story was about him.

The first telling went well. The boy listened with an open mouth, and hung his bag with slippers so unusually that she had to warn him: „That is not a hook.“ The next day, checking homework, she noticed that his **ears were clean**.

When the story came out as a picture book and when she presented it to children, something unexpected happened. In a small village in **Prigorje**, one boy felt so sick that they had to carry him out in front of the school onto a low wall. Clearly he didn't like washing his ears either. The guest concludes that she was **too drastic**. Since then, the story is always preceded by an introduction in which she explains that she made it up for her student.

From that she learned to always perform gently. If there are children with autism in the audience, she does not speak too loudly, although she is otherwise a loud person. „Everything must be rounded,“ she says. She points out that she constantly learns and seeks to improve.

sections.subtitle: Kad roditelj misli da nije maštovit: priča o Petru, Mislavu i radijatoru
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća demonstrira kako izmisliti priču iz običnog obiteljskog života
sections.content:
Iva Kraljević pita što bi poručila roditeljima koji misle da nisu maštoviti i je li važno izmišljati priče na licu mjesta ili je dovoljno čitati. Gošća odgovara jasno: **mogu to svi**.

Predlaže priče iz običnog obiteljskog života i na licu mjesta smišlja primjer. Mali **Petar** dolazi iz rodilišta, svi se okupljaju i fotografiraju ga, a on spava i nema pojma koliko mu se ljudi raduju. Kod kuće ga čeka stariji brat, recimo **Mislav**, koji se pitao kakav će brat biti. Onda Petar zaplače jer je pokakan, pa sve zasmrdi. Mislav negoduje: „Ajme, sad će on nama tu smrditi.“ Petar ponovno plače jer je gladan. Mislavu treba mama, ali mama mora dojiti maloga. Mislav se ljuti i kaže: „**Pa vratite vi tog, uzmite nekog drugog u rodilištu koji ne plače.**“ Isto tako može se pričati o Petrovu prvom rođendanu: tko je došao i što je donio.

Neka su djeca danas, kaže, sve „iznimnija“ jer imaju mnogo podražaja. Takvo dijete može zatražiti: „Tata, pričaj mi o radijatoru.“ I tada se priča može smisliti. Radijator se pokvari, dođe zima, on neće surađivati, pa u priču stigne majstor. Dalje je lakše: koji su alat izvadili, što su radili. Pričaju se **obične stvari**.

Presudan je glas. Gošća kaže da je inače puno temperamentnija, ali da joj je glas u pričanju postao nježan i blag. Zastajkuje u **dramskim tišinama**, a onda kaže „Ili!“ ili „Ali!“ i zastane. Tada je, kaže, dijete gleda.
sections.subtitle_en: When a Parent Thinks They Are Not Imaginative: The Story of Petar, Mislav, and the Radiator
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest demonstrates how to invent a story from ordinary family life
sections.content_en:
Iva Kraljević asks what she would say to parents who think they are not imaginative and whether it is important to invent stories on the spot or it is enough to read. The guest replies clearly: **everyone can do it**.

She suggests stories from ordinary family life and invents an example on the spot. Little **Petar** comes from the maternity hospital, everyone gathers and takes pictures of him, and he sleeps and has no clue how much people rejoice over him. At home his older brother waits for him, say **Mislav**, who wondered what kind of brother he would be. Then Petar cries because he has pooped, so everything starts to stink. Mislav protests: „Oh no, now he's going to stink for us here.“ Petar cries again because he is hungry. Mislav needs mom, but mom has to breastfeed the little one. Mislav gets angry and says: „**Why don't you return that one, take someone else in the maternity hospital who doesn't cry.**“ In the same way, one can talk about Petar's first birthday: who came and what they brought.

Some children today, she says, are increasingly „exceptional“ because they have many stimuli. Such a child might request: „Dad, tell me about the radiator.“ And then a story can be invented. The radiator breaks down, winter comes, it will not cooperate, so a handyman arrives into the story. From there it is easier: what tools they took out, what they did. **Ordinary things** are told.

The voice is crucial. The guest says that she is otherwise much more temperamental, but that her voice in storytelling has become gentle and mild. She pauses in **dramatic silences**, and then says „Or!“ or „But!“ and pauses. Then, she says, the child looks at her.

sections.subtitle: Mobitel u špajzi: prisutnost daje autoritet
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Horvat Vukelja savjetuje roditeljima da ostave mobitel izvan sobe dok su s djetetom
sections.content:
Iva Kraljević primjećuje da za takve stanke treba puno samopouzdanja: da tišina stvori iščekivanje, a ne prekid. Gošća upozorava da sve pada u vodu ako je mobitel pored roditelja i on gleda je li stigla poruka, možda od šefa, ili prati kako se negdje razvijaju stvari. Tada, kaže, „**taj ali ništa neće značiti**“.

Zato je roditeljima znala grubo i karikirano reći: „**Ostavite mobitel u špajzi kad ste s djetetom.**“ To znači da je mobitel utišan, da nije u istoj sobi i da ne bljeska.

Navodi i iznimke, životno važne situacije:
- kad netko čeka vijest jer hitna pomoć negdje prevozi njegova roditelja,
- kad se dijete u pubertetu, tinejdžer, nije javilo pa ga se čeka.

Sve drugo, smatra ona, može čekati. Ako je roditelj doista uz dijete, dijete će to osjetiti. Tada će i roditeljev „ali“ u priči imati **mnogo autoriteta**.
sections.subtitle_en: Mobile Phone in the Pantry: Presence Gives Authority
sections.screenshot_description_en: Željka Horvat Vukelja advises parents to leave the mobile phone outside the room while with the child
sections.content_en:
Iva Kraljević remarks that for such pauses one needs a lot of self-confidence: for the silence to create anticipation, not an interruption. The guest warns that everything falls into the water if the mobile phone is next to the parent and they look to see if a message has arrived, perhaps from the boss, or follow how things are developing somewhere. Then, she says, „**that but will mean nothing**“.

That is why she used to tell parents roughly and caricatured: „**Leave the mobile phone in the pantry when you are with the child.**“ That means the phone is muted, that it is not in the same room, and that it is not flashing.

She also cites exceptions, vitally important situations:
- when someone is waiting for news because an ambulance is transporting their parent somewhere,
- when a child in puberty, a teenager, has not called and is being waited for.

Everything else, she believes, can wait. If the parent is truly with the child, the child will feel it. Then the parent's „but“ in the story will also have **much authority**.

sections.subtitle: Zašto djeca ne žele svoje ime u priči: ježić Žinko kao zamjena
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća objašnjava zašto je bolje koristiti druga imena i životinjske likove
sections.content:
Iva Kraljević primjećuje da njezina djeca ne vole kad u priči upotrijebi njihovo ime. Kao da se unaprijed osjećaju izmanipulirano i pitaju se ide li sada neka životna lekcija. Zato to mora biti netko treći.

Gošća ima spreman odgovor: **druga imena**, a po mogućnosti junak koji preslikava neka djetetova iskustva, ali se drukčije zove i živi u drugoj ulici ili gradu. Iskustvo potvrđuje primjerom iz obitelji. Sin joj je, kao junak nekih slikovnica, rekao: „Pričaj što hoćeš, nemoj ti mene miješati u to.“ A u tom liku, priznaje, ima puno njega.

Slično vrijedi i za njezinu najnoviju knjigu **„Oratorijske zgode“**. U njoj su djevojčice s izmišljenim ili pravim imenima, ali to nisu one, nego mnogo nje same iz djetinjstva. S mnogim je stvarima, kaže, morala obračunati, ali ih ne bi stavila pod svojim imenom. U starosti, s mnogo iza sebe, čovjek je ponovno slobodan. U mladosti i zreloj dobi to ne bi učinila, a ne vole to ni djeca.

Drugo rješenje je **preseliti sve na životinjice**. Zato u njezinim knjigama ima mnogo životinjskih likova. **Mali Žinko**, nedužni ježić, kreće u školu. Tako ne mora reći da je riječ o susjedu koji se bojao škole. Djeca se s njim poistovjećuju, a životinje su, kaže, divna bića na koja se može prenijeti sve što se djeci dogodi. Roditeljima poručuje da ne brinu ako nisu originalni: važno je da priča odgovara njihovu djetetu i da nađu lik koji mu je drag.
sections.subtitle_en: Why Children Do Not Want Their Name in the Story: Hedgehog Žinko as a Substitute
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest explains why it is better to use other names and animal characters
sections.content_en:
Iva Kraljević observes that her children do not like it when she uses their name in a story. It is as if in advance they feel manipulated and wonder if some life lesson is coming now. That is why it has to be someone third.

The guest has a ready answer: **other names**, and preferably a hero who mirrors some of the child's experiences, but has a different name and lives on another street or city. She confirms the experience with an example from the family. Her son, as the hero of some picture books, told her: „Say whatever you want, don't you mix me into that.“ And in that character, she admits, there is a lot of him.

The same applies to her latest book **„Oratorijske zgode“**. In it there are girls with invented or real names, but those are not them, but rather a lot of herself from childhood. With many things, she says, she had to settle scores, but she would not put them under her own name. In old age, with a lot behind oneself, a person is free again. In youth and mature age she would not have done that, and children do not like it either.

Another solution is **to move everything onto little animals**. That is why in her books there are many animal characters. **Little Žinko**, an innocent little hedgehog, starts school. That way she does not have to say that it is about a neighbor who was afraid of school. Children identify with him, and animals are, she says, wonderful creatures onto which everything that happens to children can be transferred. She tells parents not to worry if they are not original: it is important that the story suits their child and that they find a character dear to them.

sections.subtitle: Audio bajke bez grižnje savjesti, ali uz zajedničko slušanje
sections.screenshot_description: Razgovor o kvaliteti audio bajki i zajedničkom slušanju s djecom
sections.content:
Na pitanje o audio bajkama gošća kaže: „**Sve najbolje.**“ Priznaje da ih nije puno slušala. Iva Kraljević kaže da su njezina djeca „ovisnici“ o njima i da ponekad osjeća grižnju savjesti jer bi bilo ljepše da priča mama. „Nemojte“, odgovara gošća, uz uvjet da je audio bajka kvalitetna. Ako se čuje da netko samo iščitava ili se prenemaže, to nije dobro.

Prisjeća se kako je **Jugoton** nekad izdavao krasne velike long-play ploče s dramatiziranim **Šegrtom Hlapićem** i **Pinokiom**, koje je slušala s guštom. Na **Hrvatskom radiju** postoje, kako misli, i danas, sada pod imenom **Juhuhu**, a nekad kao **Priča za laku noć**. Ondje rade najbolji glumci i fantastični redatelji, a glazba se brižljivo bira.

Ondje je i mnogo njezinih priča. Kao autorica predlagala je glazbu, primjerice Kornjaču **Saint-Saënsa** ili **uvertiru iz Carmen** za prvi dio, jer je tako „čuje“. Gotovo uvijek su je poslušali.

Dobre audio bajke imaju njezinu punu podršku. Savjetuje roditeljima da ih najprije sami preslušaju. Takva mama nije ništa lošija, ali bilo bi lijepo da za to vrijeme nije na mobitelu, nego da sluša s djecom. Ako mora obavljati poslove, neka bude **s njima u istom svijetu**. Kao posebno lijepu priliku za zajedničko slušanje ističe vožnju autom.
sections.subtitle_en: Audio Fairy Tales Without a Guilt Trip, but with Shared Listening
sections.screenshot_description_en: Conversation about the quality of audio fairy tales and shared listening with children
sections.content_en:
To the question about audio fairy tales, the guest says: „**All the best.**“ She admits she hasn't listened to them much. Iva Kraljević says that her children are „addicts“ of them and that she sometimes feels a guilt trip because it would be nicer for mom to tell stories. „Don't,“ replies the guest, on the condition that the audio fairy tale is of good quality. If it sounds like someone is merely reading off or putting on airs, that is not good.

She recalls how **Jugoton** once released wonderful large long-play records with dramatized **Šegrt Hlapić** and **Pinocchio**, which she listened to with relish. On **Hrvatski radio** they exist, as she thinks, even today, now under the name **Juhuhu**, and once as **Priča za laku noć**. The best actors and fantastic directors work there, and music is carefully selected.

Many of her stories are there too. As an author, she suggested music, for example The Tortoise by **Saint-Saëns** or the **overture from Carmen** for the first part, because that is how she „hears“ it. They almost always listened to her.

Good audio fairy tales have her full support. She advises parents to listen to them themselves first. Such a mom is no worse, but it would be nice if during that time she is not on her phone, but listens with the children. If she must do chores, let her be **with them in the same world**. As a particularly nice occasion for shared listening she highlights driving in a car.

sections.subtitle: Pažnja kao najljepši izraz ljubavi
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Horvat Vukelja govori da je pažnja najljepši dar koji možemo dati djeci
sections.content:
Iva Kraljević priznaje da je kao djevojka mlađim sestrama izmišljala priče koje „nisu ličile ni na što“. Sestre su ih ipak zapamtile, ali joj danas ponekad mozak jednostavno stane. Gošća je ohrabruje i naglašava da je ključ **ton**. Kaže da inače ne pati od „ambalaže“: okvir slike i odjeća su važni, ali ne i najvažniji. U pričanju je, međutim, ton presudan, jer dijete kroz zvuk zna da je roditelj u njemu.

Zatim izgovara jednu od ključnih misli razgovora: „**Pažnja je najljepši dar koji možemo dati djeci.**“ Dodaje da je pažnja kod djece najljepši vid iskazivanja ljubavi, i opet napominje da to nije njezina misao. Ilustrira je trenutkom u studiju. Tko joj je sada najvažniji u životu? Sugovornica. Koji joj je posao najvažniji? Ovaj, da razgovor uspije i dopre do gledatelja.

Po tome, kaže, prepoznaje „**vrhunske menadžere**“: mlade, perspektivne, pametne roditelje koji dovedu djecu i sjede u prvom redu. Poslije se hvale kako je dijete divno došlo kući. Ona ih pita jesu li slušali što je pričala. Kad pitaju kako zna, odgovara da je vidjela. Ipak ih razumije: život traži, poslodavac traži, ideje čekaju da izađu.

Njezin je savjet da u tih dvadeset minuta ili pola sata s djetetom **sve drugo prestane postojati**. To ne znači razmaziti dijete. U samoposluzi dijete neće birati sok od naranče ili marelice, kao ni goste i izlete. To treba razlikovati. Ali kad se igrate ili razgovarate, sve drugo pustite. Koliko ljubavi i potpune pažnje sada ulijete, toliko će dijete biti spremno za život. To vrijedi i za učitelje: kad ona uđe u razred, „samo je od te djece, ni od koga drugoga“.
sections.subtitle_en: Attention as the Most Beautiful Expression of Love
sections.screenshot_description_en: Željka Horvat Vukelja says that attention is the most beautiful gift we can give to children
sections.content_en:
Iva Kraljević admits that as a young girl she made up stories for her younger sisters that „looked like nothing at all“. The sisters nevertheless remembered them, but today sometimes her brain simply stops. The guest encourages her and emphasizes that the key is the **tone**. She says that otherwise she does not care about the „packaging“: the picture frame and clothing are important, but not the most important. In storytelling, however, tone is crucial, because through the sound the child knows that the parent is in it.

Then she utters one of the key thoughts of the conversation: „**Attention is the most beautiful gift we can give to children.**“ She adds that attention in children is the most beautiful form of expressing love, and again notes that this is not her thought. She illustrates it with the moment in the studio. Who is most important to her in life right now? Her interlocutor. What work is most important to her? This one, for the conversation to succeed and reach viewers.

By that, she says, she recognizes „**top managers**“: young, prospective, smart parents who bring children and sit in the front row. Afterwards they boast about how wonderfully the child came home. She asks them whether they listened to what she was saying. When they ask how she knows, she replies that she saw. Still, she understands them: life demands, the employer demands, ideas wait to come out.

Her advice is that in those twenty minutes or half an hour with the child **everything else ceases to exist**. That does not mean spoiling the child. In the supermarket the child will not choose orange juice or apricot juice, nor guests and trips. One should distinguish that. But when you play or talk, let everything else go. As much love and complete attention as you pour in now, that is how much the child will be ready for life. That applies to teachers as well: when she enters a classroom, she „belongs only to those children, to no one else“.

sections.subtitle: Don Bosko i salezijanska lekcija o prisutnosti
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća govori o otkriću Don Boska i suradnji sa salezijancima
sections.content:
Iva Kraljević sažima što je shvatila: uživljenost roditelja važnija je od same radnje i može nadomjestiti slabiju priču. Gošća potvrđuje i otkriva gdje je za to pronašla najviše potvrda: **kod salezijanaca**.

Otkrila ih je **2000. godine**, kad joj je jedan bivši „lastaš“ darovao životopis **Don Boska**. Bilo je to za nju pravo otkriće, jer za tog čovjeka nikad prije nije čula. Počela ga je proučavati, pročitala knjigu jednom, pa nakon nekoliko godina ponovno. Zatim je upoznala salezijance, koji su je, kako kaže, „hvala Bogu“, pozvali na suradnju.

Od njih stalno uči jednu stvar: **biti prisutan**. To ne vrijedi samo za djecu, nego za sve. Treba biti prisutan i uz staru majku, a ne stare „staviti u zapećak“. Priznaje da su nam stariji u svakodnevnom životu ponekad teret, ali poručuje: „Neka budu teret. **I mi smo bili njihov teret.**“

Iva Kraljević zatim najavljuje da će zajedno prelistati slikovnice i razgovarati o tome kako prepoznati dobru, a prije toga slijedi kratki promotivni segment.
sections.subtitle_en: Don Bosco and the Salesian Lesson on Presence
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest speaks about the discovery of Don Bosco and collaboration with the Salesians
sections.content_en:
Iva Kraljević summarizes what she understood: the parent's immersion is more important than the plot itself and can make up for a weaker story. The guest confirms and reveals where she found the most confirmation for that: **among the Salesians**.

She discovered them in the **year 2000**, when a former „lastaš“ gifted her a biography of **Don Bosco**. It was a real discovery for her, because she had never heard of that man before. She began studying him, read the book once, and then after several years again. Then she met the Salesians, who, as she says, „thank God“, invited her to collaborate.

From them she constantly learns one thing: **to be present**. That does not apply only to children, but to everyone. One should be present with an elderly mother too, and not „put the elderly on the back burner“. She admits that the elderly are sometimes a burden to us in everyday life, but conveys: „Let them be a burden. **We were their burden too.**“

Iva Kraljević then announces that together they will flip through picture books and discuss how to recognize a good one, and before that follows a short promotional segment.
