sections.subtitle: Raskošne slike, prazan tekst: zašto su djeca obožavala seriju Maja
sections.screenshot_description: Iva Kraljević nakon promotivnog segmenta postavlja pitanje o slikovnicama bogatih ilustracija, a siromašnog teksta
sections.content:
Nakon kratkog promotivnog segmenta, u kojem najavljivač predstavlja aplikaciju **e-duhovne vježbe** (svakodnevna razmatranja, misna čitanja, kratka razmišljanja uz Evanđelje dana i izbor molitava iz katoličke tradicije), razgovor se vraća slikovnicama. Voditeljica Iva Kraljević podsjeća da postoje minimalističke slikovnice, ali pita postoje li i one obrnute: slikovnice koje su ilustracijama vrlo bogate, a sadržajem zapravo prazne.

Željka Horvat Vukelja potvrđuje da takvih ima. Ističe da je dijete spremno u svakoj bogatoj ilustraciji pronaći nešto što mu se sviđa, *pa makar ona bila i kičasta*. Kao primjer navodi seriju koju pamti generacija koja danas ima 40, 45 ili 50 godina: **seriju Maja**, a kasnije i **seriju Sanja**, namijenjene gotovo isključivo djevojčicama. Opisuje ih kao slikovnice s vrlo lijepim djevojčicama u idiličnom okružju: topli domovi, idilične šume, cvjetnjaci, sve besprijekorno nacrtano. Tekst je, kaže, bio „nikakav“: Maja ide u šetnju, ništa joj se ne događa, ništa ne mora riješiti i nikoga posebnog ne sreće.

Odrasli su se tih slikovnica užasavali, a djeca su ih obožavala, i to upravo zbog lijepih slika. Gošća priznaje da je i svojoj kćeri kupovala tu seriju. Tekst bi letimično pročitala, a zatim bi kći njoj prepričavala kamo je Maja išla. Istodobno su kupovali i zahtjevnija izdanja, poput prvih Junakovićevih slikovnica, te seriju jednog norveškog autora s prenapučenim ilustracijama u kojima su s djecom istraživali gdje se što skriva.

Ključna je razlika, objašnjava, između ilustracija iza kojih se vidi stvaran rad i **šablona**. Priznaje da bi i ona mogla nešto preporučiti pa se poslije razočarati, ali zaključuje pomirljivo: roditelji neće pogriješiti ako ponekad kupe i pomalo kičastu slikovnicu.
sections.subtitle_en: Lavish Pictures, Empty Text: Why Children Adored the Maja Series
sections.screenshot_description_en: Iva Kraljević after the promotional segment asks a question about picture books with rich illustrations and poor text
sections.content_en:
After a short promotional segment, in which the announcer introduces the application **e-duhovne vježbe** (daily reflections, Mass readings, short thoughts on the Gospel of the day, and a selection of prayers from Catholic tradition), the conversation returns to picture books. Host Iva Kraljević reminds that minimalist picture books exist, but asks whether reverse ones also exist: picture books that are very rich in illustrations, and in content actually empty.

Željka Horvat Vukelja confirms that there are such books. She points out that a child is ready in every rich illustration to find something that appeals to them, *even if it were kitschy*. As an example, she cites the series remembered by the generation that today is 40, 45, or 50 years old: the **Maja series**, and later also the **Sanja series**, intended almost exclusively for girls. She describes them as picture books with very pretty girls in an idyllic setting: warm homes, idyllic forests, flower gardens, everything impeccably drawn. The text, she says, was „nothing“: Maja goes for a walk, nothing happens to her, she doesn't have to resolve anything, and she meets no one special.

Adults were horrified by those picture books, and children adored them, precisely because of the beautiful pictures. The guest admits that she bought that series for her daughter as well. She would read the text cursorily, and then the daughter would retell to her where Maja went. At the same time they bought more demanding editions, like Junaković's first picture books, and a series by a Norwegian author with overcrowded illustrations in which with the children they explored where things were hiding.

The key difference, she explains, is between illustrations behind which real work is seen and **templates**. She admits that she too could recommend something and later be disappointed, but concludes conciliatorily: parents will not go wrong if they sometimes buy an even somewhat kitschy picture book.

sections.subtitle: Bjeline, sitna slova i dizajnerski fontovi: što djecu odbija od slikovnice
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Horvat Vukelja objašnjava kako sitna i neobična slova otežavaju čitanje djeci početnicima
sections.content:
Na pitanje je li primijetila da djeca neke slikovnice jednostavno ne prihvaćaju, Željka Horvat Vukelja odgovara potvrdno, uz važnu ogradu: kad im se i takva knjiga predstavi na pravi način, djeca je ipak prihvate. *Moramo im dati šansu*, naglašava.

Najčešće je riječ o slikovnicama s malo sadržaja, tekstom otisnutim vrlo sitnim slovima i mnogo **bjelina**. Takve knjige, priznaje, odraslom oku izgledaju fantastično, svaka stranica djeluje kao umjetnička slika. Problem nastaje kad se dijete mora boriti sa slovima, osobito kad je dizajner odabrao neobičan font. Font može biti „stvarno zgodan“, ali dijete koje je tek naučilo čitati želi samo sudjelovati u čitanju, a takva ga slova u tome sprječavaju.

Gošća skromno napominje da nije stručnjakinja za dizajn i da o tome govori „po srcu“, te na temelju onoga što nauči slušajući pametne ljude, pa i one s čijim se mišljenjem u startu ne slaže. Zaključuje da treba biti otvoren, ali da je izbor na kraju uvijek na roditelju.
sections.subtitle_en: Whitespaces, Tiny Letters, and Designer Fonts: What Puts Children Off a Picture Book
sections.screenshot_description_en: Željka Horvat Vukelja explains how tiny and unusual letters make reading difficult for beginner children
sections.content_en:
To the question of whether she noticed that children simply do not accept some picture books, Željka Horvat Vukelja answers affirmatively, with an important qualification: when even such a book is presented to them in the right way, children nevertheless accept it. *We must give them a chance*, she emphasizes.

Most often it is picture books with little content, text printed in very tiny letters, and a lot of **whitespaces**. Such books, she admits, look fantastic to an adult eye, every page looks like an art painting. The problem arises when the child must struggle with letters, especially when the designer has chosen an unusual font. The font can be „really neat“, but a child who has just learned to read wants only to participate in reading, and such letters prevent them from doing so.

The guest modestly notes that she is not a design expert and that she speaks about it „from the heart“, and based on what she learns listening to smart people, including those whose opinion she does not agree with from the start. She concludes that one should be open, but that the choice in the end is always up to the parent.

sections.subtitle: Odgojno ili umjetnički vrijedno? Lekcija iz redakcije uz Sunčanu Škrinjarić
sections.screenshot_description: Iva Kraljević postavlja pitanje ili-ili, a Željka Horvat Vukelja bez oklijevanja odgovara
sections.content:
Iva Kraljević postavlja gošći izravno pitanje: kad bi morala birati, bi li izabrala slikovnicu koja je odgojno korisna ili onu koja je književno kvalitetna? Željka Horvat Vukelja bez oklijevanja odgovara: **odgojno korisnu**. Svjesna je da će joj „pravi umjetnici“ reći kako nije u pravu, jer i čista umjetnost predivno odgaja, ali svoj stav objašnjava urednićkim iskustvom.

U **Modroj lasti** odmah je dobila na uređivanje četiri stranice priča koje su pisali odrasli pisci, imena koja su danas u lektirama. U redakciju je redovito dolazio **Tadijanović**, i to u vrijeme dok još nije bio „maksimalno popularan“, prije nego što je, kako se približavao stotoj godini, postao tražen na sve strane. Uz takve razgovore gošća je, kako kaže, brusila vlastiti ukus.

Posebno pamti **Sunčanu Škrinjarić**, izrazito profinjenu književnicu, s kojom ju je vezala uzajamna naklonost. Škrinjarić bi je promatrala i govorila: *„Ja volim tu vašu vedrinu“*, ali bi ponekad dodala: *„Opet ste malo posrnuli urednički.“* Kad bi gošća pitala misli li na određenu priču, odgovor bi glasio da to baš nije umjetnički. Željka Horvat Vukelja branila se time da se u priči obrađuju prve bubuljice, što joj je odgojno bilo vrlo važno.

Prije četrdesetak godina o bubuljicama se u dječjoj književnosti nije pisalo. Pubertet je, kaže, bio tek malo prisutan kod **Kušana**, a začeci su se javljali kod **Krilića**. Zato je pronašla svoj omjer: oko 30 posto „lijepih“, umjetnički vrijednih priča, a 60 do 70 posto onih za koje je bila sigurna da će ih djeca pročitati i u njima prepoznati sebe. Svrha je bila da dijete shvati kako *postoji još netko tko ima bubuljice kao ja* i da to nije najgora stvar na svijetu. Voditeljica primjećuje da se dvije krajnosti ipak mogu približiti, a gošća se slaže da su upravo takva rješenja najsretnija.
sections.subtitle_en: Educational or Artistically Valuable? A Lesson from the Editorial Office with Sunčana Škrinjarić
sections.screenshot_description_en: Iva Kraljević asks an either-or question, and Željka Horvat Vukelja answers without hesitation
sections.content_en:
Iva Kraljević asks the guest a direct question: if she had to choose, would she choose a picture book that is educationally beneficial or one that is of literary quality? Željka Horvat Vukelja answers without hesitation: **educationally beneficial**. She is aware that „real artists“ will tell her she is not right, because pure art also educates wonderfully, but she explains her stance with editorial experience.

In **Modra lasta** she immediately received to edit four pages of stories written by adult writers, names that are in required reading lists today. **Tadijanović** regularly came to the editorial office, and that at a time when he was not yet „maximally popular“, before, as he approached his hundredth year, he became sought after on all sides. Along with such conversations the guest, as she says, honed her own taste.

She particularly remembers **Sunčana Škrinjarić**, an extremely refined writer, with whom she was bound by mutual affection. Škrinjarić would observe her and say: *„I love that cheerfulness of yours“*, but would sometimes add: *„You have slipped a bit editorially again.“* When the guest asked whether she meant a particular story, the reply would be that it wasn't quite artistic. Željka Horvat Vukelja defended herself by saying that the story deals with first pimples, which educationally was very important to her.

Some forty years ago pimples were not written about in children's literature. Puberty, she says, was only slightly present in **Kušan**, and beginnings appeared in **Krilić**. That is why she found her ratio: about 30 percent „beautiful“, artistically valuable stories, and 60 to 70 percent of those for which she was certain children would read them and recognize themselves in them. The purpose was for the child to realize that *there is someone else who has pimples like me* and that it is not the worst thing in the world. The host observes that the two extremes can nevertheless be brought closer, and the guest agrees that precisely such solutions are the happiest.

sections.subtitle: „Mama Pinija – Božićna želja“: dar ne mora biti materijalan
sections.screenshot_description: Voditeljica u rukama drži slikovnicu Mama Pinija – Božićna želja, a gošća objašnjava njezinu poruku
sections.content:
Voditeljica predlaže da prelistaju gošćine naslove u izdanju **Salezijane**, a Željka Horvat Vukelja izdvaja slikovnicu **„Mama Pinija – Božićna želja“**. Ističe je kao primjer knjige u kojoj su tekst i ilustracije lijepo izbalansirani, a ilustracije su „pitome, lijepe, zaobljene“.

Poruka slikovnice, objašnjava autorica, jest da se uči srcem: božićni darovi ne moraju uvijek biti materijalni, jer danas gotovo svi imaju sve. Mnogo se može učiniti malim, sitnim pažnjama prema drugima. Autorici je osobito drago kad djeca uz priču otkriju što sve živi u **mediteranskoj makiji**, oko bora koji je sam iznikao negdje u nekoj uvali. Prilikom susreta djeca joj znaju reći da je spomenula pticu čije je ime ujedno i njihovo obiteljsko prezime. Najviše je raduje upravo to što djeca sama povezuju takve stvari, iako ih nitko na to nije navodio.

Iva Kraljević primjećuje, nadovezujući se na raniju temu, koliko je font u toj slikovnici čitak. Na pitanje o dobi, autorica objašnjava da dob nigdje nije navedena, ali da je knjiga otprilike za djecu od drugog do četvrtog razreda, uz napomenu da bi htjela da i roditelji u njoj uživaju.
sections.subtitle_en: „Mama Pinija – Božićna želja“: A Gift Does Not Have to Be Material
sections.screenshot_description_en: The host holds in her hands the picture book Mama Pinija – Božićna želja, and the guest explains its message
sections.content_en:
The host suggests that they flip through the guest's titles published by **Salezijana**, and Željka Horvat Vukelja singles out the picture book **„Mama Pinija – Božićna želja“**. She points it out as an example of a book in which text and illustrations are nicely balanced, and the illustrations are „tame, beautiful, rounded“.

The message of the picture book, the author explains, is that one learns with the heart: Christmas gifts do not always have to be material, because today almost everyone has everything. Much can be done with small, tiny gestures of attention toward others. The author is especially pleased when children alongside the story discover what all lives in the **Mediterranean maquis**, around a pine tree that sprouted on its own somewhere in an inlet. During encounters, children know to tell her that she mentioned a bird whose name is also their family surname. What delights her most is precisely that children connect such things on their own, even though no one directed them to it.

Iva Kraljević observes, following up on the earlier topic, how readable the font in that picture book is. To the question about age, the author explains that age is nowhere stated, but that the book is roughly for children from second to fourth grade, with the note that she would like parents to enjoy it as well.

sections.subtitle: Paragraf ja, paragraf ti: zajedničko čitanje knjiga i stripova po ulogama
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Horvat Vukelja opisuje kako je s djecom čitala naizmjence i dijelila uloge u oblačićima stripa
sections.content:
Željka Horvat Vukelja dijeli kako je vlastitu djecu uvodila u čitanje. Sin je vrlo brzo sam naučio slova i počeo ih spajati, a zatim je došlo „vrijeme stripova“: Narednik Miki i slični junaci. Bili su toliko žestoki da je, kako kaže, *Tarzan prema njima bio kamilica*.

Tada su sklopili dogovor: jedna knjiga, pa dva-tri stripa. Za djecu početnike autorica preporučuje **tanje knjige**. U knjizi su čitali naizmjence, jedan odlomak ona, jedan sin.

S kćeri je postupala drukčije. Čitale su stripove poput *Durice* i **podijelile uloge u oblačićima**, pa je svaka čitala replike svog lika. Djeca to jako vole, naglašava gošća, ali uz jedan uvjet: uz njih mora biti roditelj, a ako ne roditelj, onda baka, teta ili susjeda.
sections.subtitle_en: A Paragraph for Me, a Paragraph for You: Joint Reading of Books and Comic Books by Roles
sections.screenshot_description_en: Željka Horvat Vukelja describes how she read alternately with her children and shared roles in comic speech bubbles
sections.content_en:
Željka Horvat Vukelja shares how she introduced her own children to reading. Her son very quickly learned letters on his own and began joining them, and then came the „comic book era“: Sergeant Mickey and similar heroes. They were so fierce that, as she says, *Tarzan compared to them was chamomile tea*.

Then they made a deal: one book, then two or three comic books. For beginner children, the author recommends **thinner books**. In the book they read alternately, one paragraph her, one her son.

With her daughter she acted differently. They read comic books like *Durica* and **divided roles in speech bubbles**, so each read the lines of her character. Children love that very much, the guest emphasizes, but under one condition: a parent must be beside them, and if not a parent, then a grandmother, aunt, or neighbor.

sections.subtitle: Chopas, Gregov dnevnik i Tom Gates: ne biti čistunac
sections.screenshot_description: Iva Kraljević opisuje sina koji ujutro sam čita Chopas stripove i pita treba li mu ih braniti
sections.content:
Voditeljica iznosi osobnu dvojbu. Njezin šestogodišnji sin, koji je tek naučio čitati, obožava **Chopas stripove**. Ujutro se probudi rano i ona ga zatekne kako u dnevnom boravku sam čita, što joj je izuzetno drago vidjeti. Ipak, u stripovima ima izraza koji joj se ne sviđaju. Pita koliko roditelji trebaju biti rigorozni, s obzirom na to da je čula kako je najvažnije da dijete zavoli knjigu.

Željka Horvat Vukelja odgovara jasno: **ne smijemo biti čistunci**. U moru ponude roditelji trebaju imati svoje kriterije, ali ne smiju dijete previše izdvajati u zaštićeni svijet. Otkriva da je i sama posudila Chopasa. Stalna je članica dječjeg odjela knjižnice u **Velikoj Gorici**, gdje posuđuje dječje knjige.

Dvije popularne serije usporedila je ovako:

- **Gregov dnevnik** isprva joj nije bio simpatičan jer glavni lik „dosta podriva stvari“ i ismijava odrasle. Danas ga smatra dobrim. U njemu prepoznaje odrasle i njihove obiteljske skupove, gdje svatko pazi tko koga gleda, pa priznaje da smo to „zaslužili“. Knjiga je pomalo subverzivna, ali je rado čita i za opuštanje.
- **Tom Gates**, engleska serija u izdanju Školske knjige, nježnija je i „suradljivija“. Također se ruga, primjerice baki koja u kolače potajno stavlja brokulu da bi bili zdravi, ali uvijek benignim stvarima. Vizualno je disperzivnija i hektičnija, no konstruktivnija i odgojnija.

Kao umirovljena učiteljica i spisateljica redovito čita tekuću hrvatsku produkciju i presretna je kad među kolegama otkrije divnu knjigu. Roditeljima savjetuje da barem zavire u ono što djeca čitaju, kao što je to učinila voditeljica: neka pročitaju nekoliko stranica Chopasa ili Gregova dnevnika. Ne trebaju biti prestrogi, ali će tako vidjeti kako funkcionira dječji um i u kojem smjeru ide.
sections.subtitle_en: Chopas, Diary of a Wimpy Kid, and Tom Gates: Not Being a Purist
sections.screenshot_description_en: Iva Kraljević describes her son who in the morning reads Chopas comic books alone and asks whether they should be forbidden to him
sections.content_en:
The host presents a personal dilemma. Her six-year-old son, who has just learned to read, adores **Chopas comic books**. In the morning he wakes up early and she finds him reading alone in the living room, which she is extremely glad to see. Nevertheless, in the comic books there are expressions she does not like. She asks how rigorous parents should be, considering she heard that the most important thing is for a child to fall in love with books.

Željka Horvat Vukelja answers clearly: **we must not be purists**. In a sea of offerings parents should have their criteria, but they must not set the child apart too much into a protected world. She reveals that she herself borrowed Chopas. She is a regular member of the children's department of the library in **Velika Gorica**, where she borrows children's books.

She compared two popular series like this:

- **Diary of a Wimpy Kid** was not appealing to her at first because the main character „undermines things quite a bit“ and mocks adults. Today she considers it good. In it she recognizes adults and their family gatherings, where everyone watches who looks at whom, so she admits that we „deserved“ it. The book is somewhat subversive, but she gladly reads it for relaxation too.
- **Tom Gates**, an English series published by Školska knjiga, is gentler and „more cooperative“. It also pokes fun, for example at a grandmother who secretly puts broccoli into cakes so they would be healthy, but always at benign things. Visually it is more dispersed and hectic, but more constructive and educational.

As a retired teacher and writer, she regularly reads current Croatian production and is overjoyed when among colleagues she discovers a wonderful book. She advises parents to at least peek into what children are reading, as the host did: let them read a few pages of Chopas or Diary of a Wimpy Kid. They need not be too strict, but that way they will see how the child's mind functions and in what direction it goes.

sections.subtitle: Igrica iz autobusa: kad djetetu servirate pritajeni strah
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Horvat Vukelja s nelagodom prepričava igricu u kojoj djevojčicu na kraju labirinta čeka opasan muškarac
sections.content:
Kontrapunkt blagom stavu prema stripovima jest primjer koji je gošću duboko uznemirio. U autobusu je vidjela kako majka djevojčici od četiri-pet godina daje igricu da je zabavi. U igrici mala junakinja hoda labirintom, sudara se sa zidovima, čuju se zvukovi, a kad dođe u slijepu ulicu, ondje je čeka **„neka ljudeskara“**, ogroman, opasan muškarac nadvijen nad prestrašenom djevojčicom. Tu taj dio igre završava i prelazi se na sljedeću razinu.

Za Željku Horvat Vukelju to je „strahota“. Pita se kakva je to poruka i kakvo je to ispunjavanje djeteta *pritajenim strahom i opasnošću*, bez ikakvog objašnjenja.

Razliku pojašnjava usporedbom s lektirom **„Ključić oko vrata“** Nikole Pulića, u kojoj se također pojavljuje sumnjiv muškarac. Ondje je, međutim, čitatelj desetogodišnjak, prije toga se vidi kako se taj lik „šmuca okolo“, a djevojčica je učinila upravo ono što su joj zabranili, upustila se u razgovor s ljubaznim nepoznatim čovjekom. Priča ima kontekst i pouku, što je nešto posve drugo od toga da se maloj djevojčici bez riječi pokaže kako je negdje čeka grozan tip. Iva Kraljević zaključuje da odrasli ponekad podcjenjuju takva dječja iskustva, misleći da dvije-tri minute ne mogu ništa promijeniti, te da treba biti oprezan.
sections.subtitle_en: The Bus Game: When You Serve a Child Lurking Fear
sections.screenshot_description_en: Željka Horvat Vukelja recounts with discomfort a game in which a dangerous man waits for a girl at the end of a maze
sections.content_en:
A counterpoint to the gentle attitude toward comic books is an example that deeply disturbed the guest. On a bus she saw a mother giving a four- or five-year-old girl a game to entertain her. In the game, the little heroine walks through a labyrinth, bumps into walls, sounds are heard, and when she comes to a dead end, waiting for her there is **„some giant brute of a man“**, a huge, dangerous man looming over the terrified little girl. There that part of the game ends and moves to the next level.

For Željka Horvat Vukelja that is a „horror“. She wonders what kind of message that is and what kind of filling a child with *lurking fear and danger* that is, without any explanation.

She clarifies the difference by comparing it to the required reading **„Ključić oko vrata“** by Nikola Pulić, in which a suspicious man also appears. There, however, the reader is a ten-year-old, before that it is seen how that character „sneaks around“, and the girl did precisely what they forbade her to do, engaged in conversation with a polite unknown man. The story has context and a moral, which is something completely different from showing a little girl without a word how a horrible guy waits for her somewhere. Iva Kraljević concludes that adults sometimes underestimate such children's experiences, thinking that two or three minutes cannot change anything, and that one needs to be careful.

sections.subtitle: „Zašto se bojala teta Darija?“: djeca hvataju antenicama
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća prepričava kako je djevojčica od cijelog druženja zapamtila samo jednu ozbiljnu rečenicu
sections.content:
Željka Horvat Vukelja priznaje da otada pažljivije promatra konkretne situacije s unucima, na druženjima na kojima su zajedno i odrasli i djeca. Djeca, kaže, registriraju i ono što ne razumiju.

Primjer je jedno okupljanje posvećeno djevojčici koja je taj dan imala „svoj dan“, iako nije bio rođendan. Razgovor je bio veseo, a samo su se u jednom kratkom segmentu odrasli dotaknuli vrlo ozbiljne teme. Prijateljica je pritom rekla rečenicu koja je počinjala s *„bojim se da…“*. Od svega je djevojčica zapamtila upravo to i poslije pitala: **„A zašto se bojala teta Darija?“** Nije bilo ničeg strašnog, objašnjava gošća, ali promijenio se glas i odrasli su se uozbiljili.

Iva Kraljević dodaje da djeca osobito osjećaju promjenu dinamike. Iz vlastitog iskustva primjećuje da se dok je dijete beba u autu može razgovarati o bilo čemu, a s djecom od tri i šest godina neke teme treba odgoditi. Gošća naglašava da roditelji nisu savršeni. Normalno je da se ponekad pred djecom „zakvače“ i posvađaju, ali moraju paziti, kao i na sadržaje koje djeci kupuju. *Promijenimo boju glasa, ozračje oko sebe, a oni sve hvataju antenicama.*
sections.subtitle_en: „Why Was Aunt Darija Afraid?“: Children Catch with Antennas
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest recounts how from the entire gathering a girl remembered only one serious sentence
sections.content_en:
Željka Horvat Vukelja admits that since then she observes more carefully concrete situations with grandchildren, at gatherings where adults and children are together. Children, she says, register even what they do not understand.

An example is a gathering dedicated to a girl who had „her day“ that day, although it was not her birthday. The conversation was cheerful, and only in one short segment did adults touch upon a very serious topic. A friend said a sentence that began with *„I'm afraid that…“*. Out of everything, the little girl remembered precisely that and later asked: **„And why was Aunt Darija afraid?“** There was nothing terrible, the guest explains, but the voice changed and the adults became serious.

Iva Kraljević adds that children especially feel a change in dynamics. From her own experience she notes that while a child is a baby in the car one can talk about anything, and with children of three and six years some topics need to be postponed. The guest emphasizes that parents are not perfect. It is normal that sometimes in front of children they „bicker“ and argue, but they must be careful, as well as with the contents they buy for children. *We change our tone of voice, the atmosphere around us, and they catch everything with their little antennas.*

sections.subtitle: „Oratorijske zgode“: prva knjiga za stariju djecu, ali i za odrasle
sections.screenshot_description: Voditeljica lista knjigu Oratorijske zgode, a gošća objašnjava kako je nastala
sections.content:
Razgovor se okreće knjizi **„Oratorijske zgode“**, prvom djelu Željke Horvat Vukelje namijenjenom starijoj djeci. Na pitanje kako je do toga došlo, autorica odgovara da je razlog divan kolektiv u **Salezijani** i ozračje koje ondje vlada. Budući da nikad nije bila u oratoriju, otišla je vidjeti kako izgleda na licu mjesta, jer nije htjela pisati o nečemu što joj je bilo „enigma“, kao što je i dalje njezinim prijateljima dok im ga ne opiše.

Zatim je spojila priče koje je godinama čuvala „u pohrani, u srcu“: iz vlastitog djetinjstva, od svojih učenika, susjedske djece i vlastite djece. Ponosna je i zadovoljna knjigom te je daruje i odraslima, uz poruku da je čitaju. Smatra je velikom knjigom i za odrasle, jer pokazuje kako djeca proživljavaju stvari i koliku ulogu odrasli mogu odigrati malim rečenicama i malim primjerima.

To se vidi već u prvoj priči, u kojoj odraslom oratorijancu, izvrsnom animatoru, majka na vrlo nježan način daje usputnu pouku o jedenju slatkoga. Autorica priznaje da se tog primjera sjeti i sama kad nepotrebno posegne za čokoladom: *kako da djeci pripovijedam, a ja se prva mašim za tim?*

Voditeljica hvali vizualno rješenje knjige s istaknutim dijelovima teksta. Autorica otkriva da je zasluga za to i jedne knjižničarke, **Julije**, koja joj je rekla da je sve lijepo, ali da knjiga mora imati slike, te joj pokazala nekoliko stranih izdanja. Autorica je potom okupila Salezijanu i ilustratoricu **Naru**, koje su se odmah složile. *Dogovorom nastaju knjige*, zaključuje, uz napomenu da treba slušati mišljenja svih koji su u lancu stvaranja knjiga za djecu.
sections.subtitle_en: „Oratorijske zgode“: The First Book for Older Children, but Also for Adults
sections.screenshot_description_en: The host flips through the book Oratorijske zgode, and the guest explains how it came about
sections.content_en:
The conversation turns to the book **„Oratorijske zgode“**, the first work by Željka Horvat Vukelja intended for older children. To the question of how that came about, the author replies that the reason is the wonderful collective at **Salezijana** and the atmosphere prevailing there. Since she had never been to an oratory, she went to see what it looks like on site, because she did not want to write about something that was an „enigma“ to her, as it continues to be to her friends until she describes it to them.

Then she combined stories that for years she kept „in storage, in the heart“: from her own childhood, from her students, neighboring children, and her own children. She is proud and pleased with the book and gifts it to adults as well, with the message that they read it. She considers it a great book for adults too, because it shows how children experience things and what a role adults can play with small sentences and small examples.

That is seen already in the first story, in which an adult oratorian, an excellent youth animator, receives from his mother in a very gentle way an incidental lesson about eating sweets. The author admits that she remembers that example herself when she unnecessarily reaches for chocolate: *how can I preach to children, when I am the first to grab for that?*

The host praises the visual design of the book with highlighted parts of the text. The author reveals that credit for that also goes to a librarian, **Julija**, who told her that everything is beautiful, but that the book must have pictures, and showed her several foreign editions. The author then gathered Salezijana and illustrator **Nara**, who immediately agreed. *Books are created by agreement*, she concludes, noting that one should listen to the opinions of everyone in the chain of creating books for children.

sections.subtitle: Od „Kruhača“ do „Nestrpljive čizmice“: kako djeci približiti kruh i svetog Nikolu
sections.screenshot_description: Iva Kraljević drži slikovnicu Kruhače i hvali njezin pristup, gošća objašnjava nastanak ideje
sections.content:
Iva Kraljević slikovnicu **„Kruhače“** naziva „genijalnom“. Djeci je, kaže, oduvijek bilo teško objasniti vrijednost kruha. Kad dijete nije htjelo jesti, roditelji su redovito spominjali „djecu u Africi“, a ova knjiga nudi mnogo ljepši pristup.

Autorica objašnjava da je ideja potekla od **Dana kruha**, koji se, otkako je Hrvatska postala samostalna, intenzivno obilježava. Smatrala je da tu lijepu manifestaciju treba malo osvježiti. Najprije je zamislila igrokaz koji nikad nije izveden, a zatim je u suradnji sa salezijancima nastala slikovnica. Te knjige imaju i drugi dio s biblijskim sadržajem. Budući da sebe ne smatra „majstorom“ za taj dio, salezijancima uvijek kaže da interveniraju gdje misle da treba, kao i kod slikovnice **„Nestrpljiva čizmica“** o svetom Nikoli, ali tako da se biblijski dio suvremeno uklopi u izmišljeni.

Najdraže joj je kad prijatelji kojima daruje slikovnicu jave: *„Joj, treći dan zaredom jedemo pohani kruh!“* Voditeljica primjećuje da je priča urodila plodom, kao i ona o dječaku koji je sutradan oprao uši. Autorica priznaje i jednu „greškicu“. Prijatelji ornitolozi upozoravaju da se ptice ne smiju hraniti kruhom, ali ona se nada da će joj oprostiti malo kruha za golubove i vrapčiće, kojima ionako nitko drugi ništa ne da.

O „Nestrpljivoj čizmici“ voditeljica kaže da ju je oduševila. Kad se približi vrijeme svetog Nikole, krene „pomama“ za Djedom Mrazom i Djedom Božićnjakom, a teško je naći nešto provjereno za katoličke obitelji. Ne smeta joj što djeca u vrtiću slušaju o Djedu Božićnjaku, ali svojoj je djeci objasnila razliku: *Djed Božićnjak je lik iz priče, poput nindža kornjače, a sveti Nikola je stvarno živio.* Kad su pitali kako onda dolazi, improvizirala je priču o anđelu čuvaru. Gošća se slaže da su „na toj pozornici“ otvoreni za sve, ali da je sveti Nikola zbilja živio. Ako bude nastavka, tajna se ni u njemu neće otkriti, jer djeci to ne treba prerano otkrivati.
sections.subtitle_en: From „Kruhače“ to „Nestrpljiva čizmica“: How to Bring Bread and Saint Nicholas Closer to Children
sections.screenshot_description_en: Iva Kraljević holds the picture book Kruhače and praises its approach, the guest explains the origin of the idea
sections.content_en:
Iva Kraljević calls the picture book **„Kruhače“** „ingenious“. For children, she says, it has always been difficult to explain the value of bread. When a child didn't want to eat, parents regularly mentioned „children in Africa“, and this book offers a much nicer approach.

The author explains that the idea originated from **Bread Day**, which, ever since Croatia became independent, has been intensively observed. She thought that this beautiful event should be refreshed a bit. First she imagined a short play that was never performed, and then in collaboration with the Salesians a picture book was created. Those books also have a second part with biblical content. Since she does not consider herself a „master“ for that part, she always tells the Salesians to intervene where they think they should, as with the picture book **„Nestrpljiva čizmica“** about Saint Nicholas, but so that the biblical part fits modernly into the fictional one.

Her favorite thing is when friends to whom she gifts the picture book report: *„Oh, for the third day in a row we are eating French toast!“* The host observes that the story bore fruit, as did the one about the boy who washed his ears the next day. The author also admits one „little error“. Ornithologist friends warn that birds must not be fed bread, but she hopes they will forgive her a little bread for pigeons and sparrows, to whom no one else gives anything anyway.

About „Nestrpljiva čizmica“ the host says that it delighted her. When the time of Saint Nicholas approaches, a „craze“ for Father Frost and Santa Claus starts, and it is hard to find something proven for Catholic families. It does not bother her that children in kindergarten hear about Santa Claus, but she explained the difference to her children: *Santa Claus is a character from a story, like a Ninja Turtle, and Saint Nicholas really lived.* When they asked how he arrives then, she improvised a story about a guardian angel. The guest agrees that „on that stage“ they are open to everyone, but that Saint Nicholas really lived. If there is a sequel, the secret will not be revealed in it either, because that need not be revealed to children too early.

sections.subtitle: Lektire pod povećalom: što je uopće mlin?
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Horvat Vukelja opisuje kako je dvoje djece pripremala za lektiru Družba Pere Kvržice
sections.content:
Voditeljica otvara temu lektira. Pita trebaju li ići u korak s vremenom, s obzirom na to da se i danas čitaju djela poput **„Vlaka u snijegu“** i **„Družbe Pere Kvržice“**, a današnja djeca vjerojatno ne znaju ni što je zadruga.

Željka Horvat Vukelja kaže da joj je tema trenutačno vrlo aktualna. Prijateljičina kći zamolila ju je za pomoć jer baka ne može na vrijeme doći iz **Zadra**, pa gošća ponekad na dva-tri sata pričuva djecu. Tako je s dvoje djece, **Jakovom** i njegovom prijateljicom, pripremala lektiru za četvrti razred: „Družbu Pere Kvržice“.

Knjigu je posudila u knjižnici i ponovno je cijelu pročitala, prvi put nakon 62-63 godine. Na svoj je užas otkrila da se likovi gotovo neprestano tuku. Porežu se pa ranu samo malo poližu i idu dalje, piju hladnu vodu dok su zagrijani. Nekad je to bilo „sve normalno“, a danas, kaže, ne bi prošlo.

Važnije joj je bilo nešto drugo: **senzibilizacija**. Fotokopirala je ilustracije i krenula od slika. Ključno pitanje bilo je *što je uopće mlin?* Djeci se brašno prodaje u dućanu i nitko od njih ne razmišlja kako zrno postaje brašno. Mlin poznaju kao ukras koji se vrti negdje u Nizozemskoj. Onda su se sjetili da su u **Lici, na Gackoj**, vidjeli mlinicu, pa je priču mogla aktualizirati.

Objasnila im je da su ljudi tada živjeli od onoga što su uzgojili na polju, za razliku od roditelja koji danas rade u bolnici ili poduzeću. Zato im je bilo važno da ne plaćaju skupo mljevenje u novom parnom mlinu, koji brzo melje, ali je skup. Imali su zapušteni mlin, a djeca su htjela i svoju „kućicu“ za igru. Tek tada su djeca bila „zrela“ za priču. Čitali su naizmjence, odlomak ona, pa Jakov, pa Rita, a kad su „zagrizli“, nastavljali su sami.
sections.subtitle_en: Required reading under the magnifying glass: what is a mill anyway?
sections.screenshot_description_en: Željka Horvat Vukelja describes how she prepared two children for the required reading Družba Pere Kvržice
sections.content_en:
The host opens the topic of required reading. She asks whether they should keep up with the times, considering that works like **„Vlak u snijegu“** and **„Družba Pere Kvržice“** are still read today, and today's children probably do not even know what a cooperative is.

Željka Horvat Vukelja says that the topic is currently very relevant to her. A friend's daughter asked her for help because the grandmother cannot arrive in time from **Zadar**, so the guest sometimes babysits the children for two or three hours. That is how she prepared the required reading for the fourth grade with two children, **Jakov** and his friend: „Družba Pere Kvržice“.

She borrowed the book from the library and read the whole thing again, for the first time after 62–63 years. To her horror, she discovered that the characters fight almost constantly. They cut themselves, then just lick the wound a little and move on, they drink cold water while they are overheated. Once upon a time, that was „all normal“, but today, she says, it would not pass.

Something else was more important to her: **sensitization**. She photocopied the illustrations and started from the pictures. The key question was *what is a mill anyway?* To children, flour is sold in a store and none of them think about how grain becomes flour. They know a mill as a decoration spinning somewhere in the Netherlands. Then they remembered that in **Lika, on the Gacka**, they had seen a watermill, so she could make the story relatable.

She explained to them that people back then lived off what they grew in the field, unlike parents who today work in a hospital or an enterprise. That is why it was important for them not to pay dearly for milling in the new steam mill, which mills quickly, but is expensive. They had an abandoned mill, and the children also wanted their own „little playhouse“. Only then were the children „ripe“ for the story. They took turns reading, a paragraph for her, then Jakov, then Rita, and when they „took the bait“, they continued on their own.

sections.subtitle: Smije li se preskakati? Od Balzaca do Proustove madlene
sections.screenshot_description: Iva Kraljević pozdravlja svoju bivšu profesoricu Marinu Čubrić, a gošća je naziva legendom
sections.content:
Gošća priznaje da je djeci rado htjela reći da neke dijelove preskoče, ali to iz pedagoških razloga nije smjela. Da se smije preskakati, prvi je put čula na fakultetu od jedne istaknute profesorice: *kad Balzac na tri stranice opisuje fasadu, smijete malo preskočiti.* Otac ju je, naprotiv, učio drukčije: zbirka priča čita se po izboru, iz zbirke pjesama čitaš one koje ti se sviđaju, „pa i pet puta“, ali roman se čita od početka do kraja.

Iva Kraljević pita provjerava li se na satu hrvatskog ponekad samo je li dijete pročitalo cijelu knjigu, a ne je li je razumjelo. Prisjeća se svoje gimnazijske profesorice **Marine Čubrić**, koju pozdravlja i naziva „totalnom kraljicom“. Gošća je poznaje i naziva je „legendom“. Profesorica Čubrić učenicima nije dopuštala preskakanje, ali bi im rekla koji se dio obrađuje. Znala je da će oni koji vole čitati ionako pročitati sve, a oni koji bi „samo nešto izmuljali“ barem će pročitati taj dio.

Željka Horvat Vukelja to pozdravlja i navodi vlastiti primjer. Kao studentica je imala čitavu francusku književnost, od srednjeg vijeka do 20. stoljeća, u šest debelih knjiga **ulomaka**. Iz **Prousta** su bili izdvojeni početak i znameniti dio o kolačiću madleni, uz slike impresionista. *Tko će čitati Prousta kad je prva rečenica duga stranicu i pol?*

Po dogovoru svoje privatne profesorice francuskog i profesorice hrvatskog dobila je zadatak da Prousta na taj način približi učenicima. Predavanje je bilo toliko „pitko“ da je došao i profesor fizike, a moralo se i ponoviti. Danas žali samo što nisu donijeli čaj i madlene za umakanje, jer bi to nekome bio *kompletan doživljaj Prousta za cijeli život*. A tko zavoli, otići će čitati sve.
sections.subtitle_en: Is skipping allowed? From Balzac to Proust's madeleine
sections.screenshot_description_en: Iva Kraljević greets her former professor Marina Čubrić, and the guest calls her a legend
sections.content_en:
The guest admits that she gladly wanted to tell the children to skip some parts, but for pedagogical reasons she was not allowed to do so. That skipping is allowed, she first heard in college from a prominent professor: *when Balzac describes a facade for three pages, you are allowed to skip a little.* Her father, on the contrary, taught her differently: a collection of stories is read by choice, from a collection of poems you read those that you like, „even five times“, but a novel is read from beginning to end.

Iva Kraljević asks whether in Croatian class it is sometimes checked only if the child has read the whole book, and not if they understood it. She recalls her gymnasium teacher **Marina Čubrić**, whom she greets and calls a „total queen“. The guest knows her and calls her a „legend“. Professor Čubrić did not allow students to skip, but she would tell them which part was being covered. She knew that those who like to read would read everything anyway, and those who would „just bluff something“ would at least read that part.

Željka Horvat Vukelja welcomes this and cites her own example. As a student, she had all of French literature, from the Middle Ages to the 20th century, in six thick books of **excerpts**. From **Proust**, the beginning and the famous part about the madeleine cake were selected, along with pictures of Impressionists. *Who will read Proust when the first sentence is a page and a half long?*

By agreement between her private French teacher and her Croatian teacher, she was given the task of bringing Proust closer to the students in that way. The lecture was so „drinkable“ that the physics teacher also came, and it had to be repeated. Today she only regrets that they did not bring tea and madeleines for dipping, because for someone that would be a *complete experience of Proust for a lifetime*. And whoever falls in love with it will go and read everything.

sections.subtitle: Mamac, udica i gumb iz močvare: uloga baka, djedova i kuma
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća objašnjava kako je djecu mamila na čitanje slikom gumba iz priče
sections.content:
Iva Kraljević primjećuje da profesori nažalost često nemaju vremena, pa bi uvođenje djece u kontekst lektire trebali preuzeti roditelji. Željka Horvat Vukelja odgovara da to od roditelja ne zahtijeva. Neka to čine ako imaju vremena i takvih aspiracija. No ako se nađe baka, umirovljena učiteljica koja voli čitati, djed, kuma svom kumčetu ili *dobrohotna prijateljica*, to su „divne stvari“.

Priznaje da će djeca možda pružiti i malo otpora, ali opisuje svoj trik. Sljedeći je put donijela sliku gumba i upitala djecu što je to. Gumb je bio trag iz priče o „duhu iz močvare“, pomoću kojeg su likovi otkrili lopova. *Udicu stavim, mamac, i eto ga*, kaže gošća.
sections.subtitle_en: Bait, hook, and a button from the swamp: the role of grandmothers, grandfathers, and godparents
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest explains how she enticed children to read with a picture of a button from the story
sections.content_en:
Iva Kraljević observes that teachers unfortunately often do not have time, so introducing children to the context of required reading should be taken over by parents. Željka Horvat Vukelja replies that she does not demand that of parents. Let them do so if they have time and such aspirations. But if there is a grandmother, a retired teacher who loves to read, a grandfather, a godmother to her godchild, or a *benevolent friend*, those are „wonderful things“.

She admits that children might also put up a little resistance, but describes her trick. The next time she brought a picture of a button and asked the children what it was. The button was a clue from the story about the „ghost from the swamp“, with the help of which the characters discovered the thief. *I cast the hook, the bait, and there you go*, says the guest.

sections.subtitle: „Peru Kvržicu ne damo iz lektire“: vječni lik za 21. stoljeće
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Horvat Vukelja s oduševljenjem opisuje Peru Kvržicu kao poduzetnog i hrabrog junaka
sections.content:
Voditeljica pita koja je to poruka „Družbe Pere Kvržice“ koja nadilazi vrijeme nastanka, jer knjiga nije postala lektira zato da bi djeca naučila što je mlin. Gošća se slaže: danas će djeca usput naučiti i što je mlin, ali najvažnije je **kakav je Pero**.

Opisuje ga kao *poduzetnog, hrabrog i punog ideja*, fantastičan i „vječan“ lik i za 21. stoljeće. Ponekad napravi i nešto što nije dobro, ali to svatko od nas ponekad učini, a njegove dobre osobine prevladavaju. *Mnogoj djeci danas fali elana. Imaju sve. A Pero nije imao ništa*, pa je sam smišljao rješenja i davao ideje. „Takvi nam ljudi trebaju“, ističe gošća. Pero drži družbu na okupu. Jedan član otpadne i to se ne riješi do kraja, „to je sve život“. Neki dođu naknadno jer vide da im je bolje u družbi, a jedan dječak svlada svoju plašljivost, što je za autoricu „slavlje“. *Peru Kvržicu ne damo iz lektire*, poručuje, uz zaključak da lektire ne bi tako lako odbacivala.

Na pitanje treba li uz klasike paralelno uvoditi i suvremene tekstove, odgovara potvrdno: barem kroz **sadržaj i ulomke**. Ako se nekoj učiteljici nešto svidi, nitko joj ne brani da to obradi s djecom. Podsjeća da je upravo zato **Modra lasta** svojedobno bila dobra: mnoge knjige koje su danas u lektiri izlazile su u njoj u skraćenom obliku, kao mini romani. Djeca danas nisu sklona časopisima, ali neke škole i dalje rade na satu s časopisima, a tako funkcionira i **SMIB**, s vrlo suvremenim temama o kojima se može polemizirati. Dodaje da se suprotstavljati mišljenja može i o Peri Kvržici.
sections.subtitle_en: „We won't let Pero Kvržica out of required reading“: an eternal character for the 21st century
sections.screenshot_description_en: Željka Horvat Vukelja enthusiastically describes Pero Kvržica as an enterprising and brave hero
sections.content_en:
The host asks what is that message of „Družba Pere Kvržice“ that transcends the time of its creation, because the book did not become required reading so that children would learn what a mill is. The guest agrees: today children will casually also learn what a mill is, but the most important thing is **what Pero is like**.

She describes him as *enterprising, brave, and full of ideas*, a fantastic and „eternal“ character for the 21st century as well. Sometimes he also does something that is not good, but each of us does that sometimes, and his good traits prevail. *Many children today lack drive. They have everything. And Pero had nothing*, so he came up with solutions and gave ideas himself. „We need such people“, the guest emphasizes. Pero holds the group together. One member drops out and that is not resolved to the end, „that is all life“. Some join subsequently because they see that it is better for them in the group, and one boy overcomes his timidity, which for the author is a „celebration“. *We won't let Pero Kvržica out of required reading*, she says, concluding that she would not discard required reading so easily.

To the question of whether contemporary texts should be introduced in parallel with classics, she replies affirmatively: at least through **content and excerpts**. If a teacher likes something, nobody forbids her to cover it with children. She reminds that that was precisely why **Modra lasta** was good in its day: many books that are in required reading today were published in it in an abridged form, as mini-novels. Children today are not inclined toward magazines, but some schools still work with magazines in class, and **SMIB** functions the same way, with very contemporary topics about which one can debate. She adds that opinions can also be confronted about Pero Kvržica.

sections.subtitle: Nikakve zabrane: „Dobrim potisnuti loše“ i koš umjesto trgovačkog centra
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća kritizira trgovačke centre koji niču na mjestu livada i igrališta
sections.content:
Iva Kraljević pita je li gošća ikad poželjela da se neka lektira makne s popisa. Odgovor je kratak: **„Nikad.“** Željka Horvat Vukelja kaže da nije za zabrane ni u kojem obliku, čak ni kad joj se nešto ne sviđa. Umjesto toga traži što bi mogla predložiti od dobroga. Njezino je staro geslo, slično jednoj misli koju je pronašla i kod salezijanaca: **dobrim potisnuti loše**.

Tu misao proširuje na stariju djecu i mlade. Svi govore kako se mladi odaju porocima, a gošća pita *što im mi nudimo?* U naseljima gleda kako na mjestu livada niču novi trgovački centri, jedan za drugim, a slijepe ulice probijaju se kako bi se brže stiglo do njih. Mladima se pritom miču koševi i igrališta. Za mali nogomet u kavezu („cage“) u svom naselju, gdje mladi „igraju kao ludi“, kaže da je *jako odrešita*: to se ne smije maknuti.

Predlaže i nekoliko konkretnih stvari:

- djeci treba davati dobre sadržaje koji zaokupljaju misli, ruke i noge;
- treba ih uključivati u **kućne poslove**, pa makar ih obavili traljavo. Neka operu prozor i kroz kolobare se jedva vidi, „pa što onda?“;
- treba ih pustiti da troše mladenačku energiju na korisne stvari, jer se tako potiskuje zlo.

Nije protiv jumbo plakata i kampanja, jer i toga treba biti, ali na njih ode mnogo novca. *Možda bi bolje bilo izgraditi negdje jedan koš* ili napraviti betonski stol za stolni tenis. Upravo ju je takav pristup, kaže, privukao salezijancima.
sections.subtitle_en: No bans whatsoever: „Suppressing the bad with the good“ and a basketball hoop instead of a shopping center
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest criticizes shopping centers springing up in place of meadows and playgrounds
sections.content_en:
Iva Kraljević asks whether the guest has ever wished for some required reading to be removed from the list. The answer is short: **„Never.“** Željka Horvat Vukelja says that she is not in favor of bans in any form, even when she does not like something. Instead, she looks for what good she could propose. Her old motto, similar to a thought she also found with the Salesians: **to suppress the bad with the good**.

She extends that thought to older children and youth. Everyone talks about how young people indulge in vices, and the guest asks *what are we offering them?* In residential neighborhoods, she watches new shopping centers sprout in place of meadows, one after another, and cul-de-sacs are broken through to reach them faster. At the same time, basketball hoops and playgrounds are removed from young people. Regarding cage football in her neighborhood, where young people „play like crazy“, she says she is *very resolute*: that must not be removed.

She also proposes several concrete things:

- children should be given good content that engages the mind, hands, and legs;
- they should be included in **household chores**, even if they do them sloppily. Let them wash a window and one can barely see through the streaks, „so what?“;
- they should be allowed to spend youthful energy on useful things, because in that way evil is suppressed.

She is not against billboards and campaigns, because those are needed too, but a lot of money is spent on them. *Maybe it would be better to build a basketball hoop somewhere* or make a concrete table for table tennis. Precisely such an approach, she says, attracted her to the Salesians.
keywords_en: suppressing the bad with the good

sections.subtitle: Salezijana na Interliberu i knjiga kao dar
sections.screenshot_description: Iva Kraljević najavljuje štand Salezijane na Interliberu
sections.content:
Voditeljica najavljuje da će **Salezijana** uskoro izlagati na **Interliberu**, ovaj put s nešto raskošnijim štandom, iako je i prošli bio vrlo lijep, te pita hoće li i gošća biti ondje. Željka Horvat Vukelja odgovara da uvijek dođe u neko doba, prema dogovoru s izdavačem, kojem daje „svekoliku podršku“. Salezijanu opisuje kao krasnog izdavača i dobru ekipu koja je nikad nije razočarala. Dodaje da se ljudi u životu ponekad međusobno razočaraju, ali da dobre stvari prevladaju. Iva Kraljević se slaže i ističe odlične naslove, uključujući i gošćine.

Gošća otkriva da knjige rado **daruje**. Kupuje ih djeci i od drugih dobrih izdavača, a od Školske knjige, u kojoj je radila, ima mnogo „divot izdanja“. Salezijanine naslove daruje i odraslima, jer otprilike zna kome što treba. Voditeljica zaključuje da je knjiga lijep, ali i vrlo koristan dar.
sections.subtitle_en: Salezijana at Interliber and a book as a gift
sections.screenshot_description_en: Iva Kraljević announces the Salezijana booth at Interliber
sections.content_en:
The host announces that **Salezijana** will soon exhibit at **Interliber**, this time with a somewhat more lavish booth, although the last one was also very beautiful, and asks whether the guest will also be there. Željka Horvat Vukelja replies that she always comes at some point, according to an agreement with the publisher, to whom she gives „all-around support“. She describes Salezijana as a wonderful publisher and a good team that has never disappointed her. She adds that in life people sometimes disappoint one another, but that good things prevail. Iva Kraljević agrees and highlights excellent titles, including the guest's.

The guest reveals that she gladly **gifts** books. She buys them for children from other good publishers as well, and from Školska knjiga, where she worked, she has many „deluxe editions“. She also gifts Salezijana's titles to adults, because she roughly knows who needs what. The host concludes that a book is a beautiful, but also a very useful gift.

sections.subtitle: Što su je djeca naučila: jednostavnost, iskrenost i istinska zaigranost
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Horvat Vukelja govori o lekcijama koje je naučila od djece
sections.content:
Pred kraj razgovora Iva Kraljević gošću naziva „prozorom u dječji svijet“, jer djecu nije samo poučavala, nego ih je i slušala, čitala njihova pisma i pratila njihove reakcije. Pita je koju je životnu lekciju naučila od djece.

Željka Horvat Vukelja navodi najprije **jednostavnost**, zatim **iskrenost** i **autentičnost**. Bezbrižnosti je djeca, kaže, ne mogu naučiti, jer odrasli imaju brige i „puno šire antene“. Ali od njih „pije“ onu trenutačnu, istinsku opuštenost u igri. *Kad se igraš, onda se igraš*, pa odraslome neće biti glupo igrati „Čovječe, ne ljuti se“ ili smisliti neku njegovu inačicu.

Otkriva da je izmislila mnoštvo igara, najprije dok je radila u Školskoj knjizi, a danas privatno. S djecom igra i **jamb prilagođen djeci**, a pritom se, kaže, sve ori dok se viče, dobiva, gubi i tuguje. Na primjedbu voditeljice da za to treba energije odgovara da je u mirovini i slobodna, ali da ne želi to nuditi kao recept. Zaključuje da je biti odgajatelj težak poziv, a biti učitelj nezahvalan, *ali divan*.
sections.subtitle_en: What children have taught her: simplicity, sincerity, and true playfulness
sections.screenshot_description_en: Željka Horvat Vukelja talks about the lessons she learned from children
sections.content_en:
Toward the end of the conversation, Iva Kraljević calls the guest a „window into the children's world“, because she did not only teach children, but also listened to them, read their letters, and followed their reactions. She asks her what life lesson she learned from children.

Željka Horvat Vukelja mentions first **simplicity**, then **sincerity** and **authenticity**. Children cannot, she says, teach her carefreeness, because adults have worries and „much wider antennas“. But from them she „drinks“ that momentary, true relaxation in play. *When you play, then you play*, so it will not feel silly for an adult to play „Ludo“ or come up with some version of it.

She reveals that she invented a multitude of games, first while working at Školska knjiga, and today privately. With children she also plays **Yahtzee adapted for children**, and in doing so, she says, everything echoes while shouting, winning, losing, and grieving. To the host's remark that this takes energy, she replies that she is retired and free, but that she does not want to offer this as a recipe. She concludes that being an educator is a difficult calling, and being a teacher ungrateful, *but wonderful*.

sections.subtitle: Najvažniji savjet roditeljima: budite svoji uz dječji krevetić
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća daje završni savjet roditeljima koji misle da nemaju mašte
sections.content:
Na pitanje koji bi jedan savjet o pričanju priča dala roditeljima, Željka Horvat Vukelja obraća se *svima koji misle da nemaju mašte i da nisu majstori*. Kad navečer sjednu uz krevetić ili krevet svoje djece, nitko ne zna što pričaju. Ne mora ih brinuti hoće li netko reći da je to smiješno ili naivno. I njoj, kaže, za mnogo toga govore da je naivna, a to uopće nije bitno.

**„Dajte si oduška. Budite svoji.“** To su roditeljima možda jedni od rijetkih trenutaka u danu kad su doista svoji, a dijete će biti presretno jer će znati da mu daju istinski dio sebe. Gošća se pritom vraća vlastitom iskustvu: upravo su joj to davali njezini roditelji, a takvo nešto je, kaže, *zalog za cijeli život*. Poruka je jednostavna: ne treba brinuti što niste stručni, dovoljno je posvetiti vrijeme i pažnju.
sections.subtitle_en: The most important advice to parents: be yourself by the child's crib
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest gives concluding advice to parents who think they have no imagination
sections.content_en:
To the question of what single piece of advice about storytelling she would give to parents, Željka Horvat Vukelja addresses *everyone who thinks they have no imagination and that they are not masters*. When in the evening they sit beside their children's crib or bed, nobody knows what they are telling. They do not have to worry whether someone will say that it is funny or naive. She says that people call her naive for many things too, and that does not matter at all.

**„Let yourselves go. Be yourselves.“** For parents, those are perhaps some of the rare moments in the day when they are truly themselves, and the child will be overjoyed because they will know that they are giving them a true part of themselves. In doing so, the guest returns to her own experience: that is precisely what her parents gave her, and such a thing is, she says, *a pledge for a lifetime*. The message is simple: there is no need to worry that you are not experts, it is enough to dedicate time and attention.

sections.subtitle: Vrapčić, personalizirane slikovnice i rođenje „slikopriče“
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Horvat Vukelja govori o trenutačnom radu i o tome kako je smislila naziv slikopriča
sections.content:
Iva Kraljević zahvaljuje gošći na vremenu i pažnji, za koju kaže da ju je cijelo vrijeme osjećala, te je pita na čemu trenutačno radi. Željka Horvat Vukelja kaže da „se blokić puni“. Na svojoj web-stranici povremeno objavljuje slikopriče, a najsretnija je kad nastanu prema istinitom događaju, iako pisac uvijek mora ponešto promijeniti.

Jedna takva nastala je kad su joj curice iz naselja donijele **vrapčića koji je ispao iz gnijezda**, da ga spasi. U šali dodaje da su time njoj i kćeri natovarile probleme na glavu, ali sve je sretno završilo. Iz toga je nastala mala slikopriča, a za djevojčice i **personalizirane slikovnice**: u sredini je slikopriča s njezinim crtežima i rukom pisanim slovima, a izvana fotografije djevojčica i vrapčića. To ostaje samo njima i ne objavljuje se, jer je, kaže, riječ o privatnosti. Iz takvih malih stvari onda se iskristalizira i nešto veće.

Voditeljica podsjeća na zanimljivost da je upravo gošća smislila naziv **slikopriča**, koji se danas posve uvriježio. Autorica s ponosom kaže da je postao opća imenica. Kad je tadašnju urednicu **Slavenku Halačev** pitala smije li ga upotrijebiti, odgovor je bio: *„Smije. Baš je krasno.“* Halačev opisuje kao disciplinirana, urednog, klasičnog urednika sa znatnim osjećajem za novo. Iva Kraljević dodaje da i njezina djeca vole slikopriče te da je jednu pročitala baš tog jutra.

Na rastanku gošća zahvaljuje na lijepim pitanjima i strpljivom slušanju. Priznaje da se na putu molila *„Bože, molim te da ne pričam previše“*, a na kraju je ipak bila opširna, uvjerena da će i nakon montaže ostati mnogo dobroga. Voditeljica odgovara da s njezine strane nije bilo ni riječi viška. Poziva gledatelje na **Interliber** od 10. do 15. studenoga, gdje Salezijana ima štand u šestom paviljonu s naslovima po sniženim cijenama, a ondje se možda mogu susresti i sa Željkom Horvat Vukeljom.
sections.subtitle_en: A little sparrow, personalized picture books, and the birth of the „slikopriča“
sections.screenshot_description_en: Željka Horvat Vukelja speaks about her current work and about how she coined the term slikopriča
sections.content_en:
Iva Kraljević thanks the guest for her time and attention, which she says she felt the entire time, and asks her what she is currently working on. Željka Horvat Vukelja says that „the notebook is filling up“. On her website she occasionally publishes slikopriče, and she is happiest when they are created according to a true event, although a writer must always change something.

One such came about when the little girls from the neighborhood brought her **a little sparrow that had fallen out of the nest**, so that she would save it. In jest, she adds that with this they heaped problems on her and her daughter's heads, but everything ended happily. From this a small slikopriča arose, and for the girls also **personalized picture books**: in the middle is the slikopriča with her drawings and handwritten letters, and on the outside photos of the girls and the little sparrow. That remains only for them and is not published, because, she says, it is a matter of privacy. From such small things something bigger then crystallizes.

The host recalls the interesting fact that it was precisely the guest who coined the term **slikopriča**, which is completely common today. The author proudly says that it has become a common noun. When she asked the then editor **Slavenka Halačev** if she was allowed to use it, the answer was: *„You are. It is really lovely.“* She describes Halačev as a disciplined, neat, classic editor with a considerable sense for the new. Iva Kraljević adds that her children also love slikopriče and that she read one that very morning.

At parting, the guest thanks for the nice questions and patient listening. She admits that on the way she prayed *„God, please let me not talk too much“*, and in the end she was nonetheless extensive, convinced that even after editing a lot of good will remain. The host replies that on her part there was not a word too many. She invites viewers to **Interliber** from November 10 to 15, where Salezijana has a booth in the sixth pavilion with titles at discounted prices, and there one can perhaps also meet Željka Horvat Vukelja.
